books.title: You're a Jellyfish!
books.art_why: Jellyfish are real ocean animals alive today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Floating at Sea Imagine that your body is shaped like a bell, and you have long tentacles streaming down under you. You are mostly made of water and cannot survive away from it. You live in the ocean and travel by floating gracefully on currents. You’re a jellyfish, or jelly, and not a fish at all. You’re a kind of invertebrate —an animal that has no backbone.
pages.brief: A single jellyfish floats in open blue ocean water, its soft bell-shaped body pulsing near the surface and long thin tentacles streaming down beneath it. Sunlight filters through the water around it as it drifts on a gentle current.

pages.text: You and your jellyfish cousins live in every ocean in the world. Some also live in lakes and ponds. Some live in warm water, and others prefer cold water. Some of your cousins are survivors—they’ve been around for 650 million years, since long before the time of dinosaurs.
pages.brief: Several different jellyfish drift in cool blue water: one in a warm shallow sea, one in cold dark water, and small jellies in a calm lake. Their bells and trailing tentacles show the many places these animals live around the world.

pages.text: Jelly Bodies Like all jellyfish, you have no brain, heart, blood, or bones. Your body is made of water, muscles, and nerves. You use your eyespots and nerve network to sense up and down, light and dark, and the world around you. The main part of your body is your bell. Tentacles hang from around your edges like fringe. A mouth and digestive sac hang in the center. Some of your cousins have frilly oral arms, or mouth arms, around this sac.
pages.brief: A close view of one jellyfish. Its rounded bell is the main body, with short tentacles fringing the edge like a border. In the center hangs a small mouth and digestive sac, and a few frilly mouth arms curl around it.

pages.text: Do You Know? The smallest jellyfish is as tiny as a pearl. The largest jellyfish is the lion’s mane jellyfish. Its bell is wider than the length of a bed. Its tentacles can be as long as a school bus! You and your cousins come in many shapes, sizes, and colors. Jellyfish that live near the ocean’s surface are often clear, or see- through. Jellies that live deep in the ocean may be red or purple. Some jellies are white with splashes of color. Some deep-sea jellyfish even glow in the dark!
pages.brief: A tiny pearl-sized jellyfish beside a huge lion's mane jellyfish whose wide bell is broader than a bed and whose tentacles trail as long as a school bus. Nearby, a clear see-through jelly drifts at the surface and a red-purple jelly glows in deep dark water.

pages.text: Getting Around As a jellyfish, you spend most of your time drifting on ocean currents. But you can also move when you want to. First you let your bell fill with water. Then you squeeze the muscles in your bell the way a person blows a bubble with bubble gum. As you force water out of your bell, you shoot forward.
pages.brief: A jellyfish in mid-swim, its bell squeezed tightly closed as it forces water out behind it and shoots forward through the blue ocean, leaving a small ripple of moving water in its wake.

pages.text: Some of your jellyfish cousins swim close to the ocean’s surface to bask in sunlight. Others avoid light and stay deeper in the ocean. Some live in the open ocean, while others stay closer to shore. Like all jellyfish, you are not a social animal. But divers and scientists often find your kind in large groups. You and the other jellies aren’t enjoying each other’s company. You just happen to be in the same place at the same time. You’re a Jellyfish!
pages.brief: Two divers with tanks float among a large group of jellyfish gathered in open water, some near the sunlit surface, others deeper down. Near shore, more jellies drift close to the sandy bottom in shadowed water.

pages.text: Life Cycle You began your jellyfish life as an egg released into water by your mom. After your dad fertilized the egg, it grew into a tiny wormlike animal called a planula (PLAN- yoo-luh). The planula floated in water for a few weeks. Then it attached to a rock and developed into a polyp (PAHL-ip). Over time, the polyp cloned itself through a process called budding. It grew disks that popped off, swam away, and developed into adult jellyfish. One of those adults, or medusas (muh-DOO-suz), is you! Life Cycle of a Jellyfish.
pages.brief: Stages of jellyfish growth shown across one scene: a tiny egg in water, a small wormlike planula floating, a polyp stuck to a rock, disks budding off the polyp, and at the end an adult medusa swimming free with its bell and tentacles.

pages.text: Do You Know? One kind of jellyfish grows its own food. The upside-down jellyfish lies on the bottom of shallow warm oceans. It eats algae and then grows more just by sitting in the sunlight. Hunter and Hunted Like other jellyfish, you like to eat fish, crabs, shrimp, and tiny marine animals. The key to successful hunting is the stinging cells in your tentacles. You catch prey as it floats through the water. Some of your cousins also have a glow that attracts fish. Others have a sticky gel that catches animals passing by. You’re a Jellyfish!
pages.brief: An upside-down jellyfish rests on the sandy bottom of a warm shallow sea, lying in bright sunlight among green algae. Beside it, a hunting jellyfish trails stinging tentacles that catch a small fish and a shrimp drifting past.

pages.text: Many animals avoid eating you and your cousins. After all, who wants a mouthful of stinging cells? But some animals don’t seem to mind at all. Sea turtles and some fish and birds think of jellyfish as a real treat. You try hard to protect yourself from being eaten by hiding or by stinging. Still, many of your cousins are eaten while they are still growing or as adults.
pages.brief: A sea turtle with its mouth open bites a jellyfish, and nearby fish and a seabird also feed on jellies. Other jellyfish pull their tentacles in and sink lower into the water, trying to hide from the animals hunting them.

pages.text: Do You Know? A jellyfish called the Australian sea wasp is one of the most poisonous animals in the world. A sting can kill a person in three minutes. People and Jellyfish People often see your jellyfish cousins on beaches. Sadly, those jellies are either dead or dying. People need to remember to never touch a jellyfish! Even a dead jelly can sting. Most of your jellyfish cousins have a mild sting that is painful and causes a red rash. But the sting of some jellies can be deadly. You’re a Jellyfish!
pages.brief: On a sandy beach, people walk past jellyfish washed up at the water's edge and keep their hands away. Offshore, the pale Australian sea wasp jellyfish drifts with its long tentacles trailing in the sea.

pages.text: Jellyfish Stings Symptoms: • Intense stinging pain • Red rash • Swollen, raised patches of skin • Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea • Fever, chills, and sweating • Back and abdominal pain Treatment: • Rinse with seawater (not fresh water). • Don’t rub the wound or apply ice. • Apply white vinegar to the wound. • Remove tentacles using gloves, a heavy cloth, or tweezers. • Stay as still as possible to keep the poison from spreading. • See a doctor right away in case of breathing problems, severe pain, or other intense symptoms.
pages.brief: A close view of a person's bare arm and leg showing a red, swollen, raised rash. Seawater is poured over the stung skin from a container, and a pair of gloved hands lifts a thin tentacle away with tweezers.

pages.text: Conclusion Scientists learn new facts about jellyfish every year. They also often discover new kinds of jellies. In 2003, a large red jellyfish that has no tentacles was discovered off the coast of California. People enjoy looking at jellyfish at zoos or aquariums. Watching you gently float through water is fun and relaxing. Even without brains, your cousins must be pretty smart to have survived for millions of years! You’re a Jellyfish!
pages.brief: Scientists on a boat look at a large red jellyfish with no tentacles brought up from the sea off a California coast. In a dim aquarium, visitors stand watching jellyfish gently float and pulse through the lit blue water.

books.title: Weird Bird Beaks
books.art_why: Real birds and their beaks can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: Bearded Barbet I am a bearded barbet, as you can see from the hairlike feathers that look like a beard on my beak. My large, thick beak also has pointed parts on the bottom like sharp teeth. I live where it is dry in Africa. I am a member of the woodpecker family. Like the woodpecker, I often use my tail feathers to help me hold onto trees. I use my beak to make a hole in a dead tree or stump to build my nest. I feed on fruit and sometimes on insects. I live with a partner and three or four other birds that help incubate our eggs and care for the chicks after they hatch.
pages.brief: A bearded barbet clings to a tree in dry Africa, its hairlike beak feathers looking like a beard. The bird has a large, thick beak with pointed parts underneath. It uses its tail feathers for support and its beak to make a nest hole in a dead tree or stump. Fruit and insects are nearby.

pages.text: Crossbill I am a type of finch called a crossbill because my beak is crossed like an X, which helps me pull the seeds out of pinecones. I hold a cone with one foot and then pry open the scales of the cone to get the pine nuts. Pinecones grow on trees called conifers, but conifers don’t produce good pinecones every year, so I travel all over to find pinecones instead of living in one place. If I can’t find any pine nuts to eat, I will settle for other seeds and even insects to survive. Like the canary, which I’m related to, I sing beautiful and elaborate melodies.
pages.brief: A crossbill finch perches in a conifer, holding a pinecone with one foot. Its beak is crossed like an X as it pries open the cone’s scales to reach pine nuts. The bird travels to find good pinecones and will eat other seeds or insects. It sings a beautiful, elaborate melody.

pages.text: Rhinoceros Hornbill I am called a rhinoceros hornbill because of the horn on top of my beak, which I use to knock down fruit. I also use my horn to fight and sometimes to attract a mate. When my mate is incubating eggs in a tree-hole nest, I seal her in with mud. I leave a small opening in the mud for my beak to fit through so that I can bring her food. She breaks out once our babies hatch, but then we seal them in again for safety until they are old enough to leave the nest. If you think my horn looks weird, you should see my eyelashes! I am one of the few birds that have them.
pages.brief: A rhinoceros hornbill stands by a tree-hole nest, showing the horn on top of its beak. The horn is used to knock down fruit, fight, and attract a mate. The male seals the incubating female inside with mud, leaving a small opening to bring her food. The bird has unusual eyelashes.

pages.text: Huia We huias (HOO-yuhs) lived in New Zealand until we became extinct. “I am the male. My beak is thick and strong.” “I am the female. My beak is thin and curved.” Our beaks were so different that for a long time, people thought we weren’t related to each other at all. We looked alike otherwise, though, with orange fleshy wattles and shiny black feathers except for the white tips of our tails. We ate insects and insect larvae, spiders, and sometimes berries.
pages.brief: A male and female huia stand together in New Zealand, now extinct. The male has a thick, strong beak; the female has a thin, curved beak. Otherwise they look alike, with orange fleshy wattles, shiny black feathers, and white tail tips. Insects, larvae, spiders, and berries are nearby.

pages.text: Sword-Billed Hummingbird I am a sword-billed hummingbird, a very small bird with a very long beak. In fact, I’m the only bird with a bill longer than my body. My beak is heavy, so when I land, I tilt my head up to reduce the strain on my neck. I use my long beak and even longer tongue to get nectar from tube-shaped flowers. I can stick my tongue out and pull it back in again about 13 times per second. I live in the Andes Mountains of South America, where I build my nest of moss and leaves held together with cobwebs.
pages.brief: A tiny sword-billed hummingbird hovers by tube-shaped flowers in the Andes Mountains. Its long, heavy beak is longer than its body; when it lands, it tilts its head up. It uses its long tongue to sip nectar, flicking it in and out about thirteen times per second. Its nest is moss and leaves held with cobwebs.

pages.text: Brown Pelican I am a brown pelican. I have a pouch of skin under my beak that can hold almost three gallons of water and fish! I hunt in the ocean, diving down into the water from the air, although I’m not above taking fish from fishing boats. I sometimes steal fish from other birds, but they steal from me, too. Gulls even sit on my head and back while they take fish right out of my pouch! I have webbed feet. I use them to warm my eggs, unlike most birds, which use their breasts.
pages.brief: A brown pelican dives into the ocean, its beak pouch stretched wide. The pouch can hold almost three gallons of water and fish. The pelican hunts by diving from the air and may take fish from fishing boats or other birds. Gulls sit on its head and back to steal fish. It warms its eggs with webbed feet.

pages.text: Shoebill Stork I am called a shoebill stork because my beak is shaped like a shoe but with a hook on the end that helps me eat fish. I hunt fish by waiting for one to swim by and then falling onto it with my mouth open. Sometimes I’ll eat frogs and even small crocodiles. I live in the swamps and marshes of Africa. I have one mate for life. We don’t really hang out with other shoebill storks unless food is scarce. We share the work of parenting, including keeping our eggs cool by dousing them with mouthfuls of water and surrounding them with wet grass. Even after our chicks are born, we keep cooling them off until they grow their own feathers.
pages.brief: A shoebill stork stands in an African swamp, showing its shoe-shaped beak with a hook at the end. It waits for a fish to swim by, then falls onto it with its mouth open. It may also eat frogs and small crocodiles. With its mate, it cools its eggs and chicks using mouthfuls of water and wet grass.

pages.text: Spoonbill I am called a spoonbill because I have a long beak that flattens out at the end like a spoon. People often confuse me with a flamingo because of my white and pink color, but not after they see my bill, which looks nothing like a flamingo’s. To find food, I sweep my bill back and forth in the mud and shallow water, using touch more than sight to hunt. When I feel something bump against my beak, I snatch it up. I like to eat frogs, shellfish, seaweed, and small fish. I regurgitate my food into my babies’ mouths back at the nest.
pages.brief: A spoonbill wades in shallow water and mud, sweeping its long, spoon-shaped bill back and forth. It hunts by touch, snatching up frogs, shellfish, seaweed, and small fish when they bump its beak. Its white and pink coloring may look like a flamingo’s, but its bill is different. At the nest, it regurgitates food into its babies’ mouths.

pages.text: Toucan I am a toucan, and I have a huge and colorful beak that is actually very light because it’s full of air pockets. I eat fruit, seeds, insects, eggs, and sometimes lizards. My beak helps me reach fruit while I sit in rainforest trees, and to toss it back and forth with another toucan as part of a mating ritual. I can also use my beak to skin the fruit. I have two claws that point forward and two that point backward to help me hold onto branches. My nest is in a tree hole. Baby toucans take several months to grow the large beak typical of adult toucans.
pages.brief: A toucan sits in a rainforest tree, holding fruit with its huge, colorful beak. The beak is light because it is full of air pockets. It reaches and skins fruit, and tosses it with another toucan. Two claws point forward and two backward grip the branch. Its nest is in a tree hole; babies take months to grow adult beaks.

pages.text: As you can see, many birds have weird beaks. Some beaks help birds to catch or eat their food. Other beaks just look incredible. Which beak is your favorite?
pages.brief: Several birds with weird beaks are shown together in natural surroundings. Some beaks are shaped for catching or eating food while others simply look incredible. The birds display a variety of unusual beak shapes and colors. The scene invites viewers to look closely and pick a favorite beak.

books.title: Expedition Zero
books.art_why: Modern-day Singapore, Java, Bali, Brazil, Congo and Kenya all exist today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Getting Ready for Your Trip Pack light clothes and a hat to protect yourself from the Sun. Also, take insect repellent —the bugs are big where you’re going. Throw in an umbrella because it rains often. Don’t forget a camera; you might see monkeys, parrots, or pythons. You will be traveling at zero degrees latitude along the equator (ee-KWAY-ter), the imaginary line that separates the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
pages.brief: A traveller packs a small bag for a trip. Laid out ready are light clothes, a wide-brimmed hat for protection from the Sun, a bottle of insect repellent, a folded umbrella and a camera, in case monkeys, parrots or pythons appear.

pages.text: Starting Out in Singapore As your plane nears the airport in Southeast Asia, you look down on Singapore. Its shiny skyscrapers make this small island country look very large. You can see hundreds of ships in the harbor. Singapore has one of the world’s busiest ports.
pages.brief: Through an airplane window a passenger looks down as the plane nears the airport. Below lies Singapore, a small island country crowded with shiny skyscrapers, so it looks very large. Hundreds of ships fill the harbour, one of the world's busiest ports.

pages.text: As you begin to explore the city, the tropical heat takes your breath away. You come upon an outdoor market. You can tell that you are in a hot climate by looking at the plants for sale. Sugar cane, limes, papayas, and orchids love Singapore’s hot, wet weather. The charts below show what the climate is like at one degree north latitude. Average Monthly Temperatures in Singapore • January, 85°F • February, 87°F • March, 88°F • April, 89°F • May, 88°F • June, 88°F Average Monthly Precipitation in Singapore • January, 7.8 inches • February, 6.1 inches • March, 6.7 inches • April, 5.6 inches • May, 6.2 inches • June, 5.5 inches.
pages.brief: In breath-taking tropical heat, a person explores an outdoor market. Stalls display plants for sale: tall stalks of sugar cane, baskets of limes, ripe papayas and blooming orchids. Everyone moves slowly in Singapore's hot, wet weather.

pages.text: Island Hopping in Indonesia Your next stop is Java, one of Indonesia’s thousands of islands. You’re traveling on a train without air-conditioning through the lowlands. It’s hot! In the distance, the tops of volcanoes poke above the clouds. You pass paddies—watery fields where rice is grown. The volcanic soil is good for growing crops.
pages.brief: A traveller rides an old train without air-conditioning through the hot lowlands of Java. Out of the window stretch watery rice paddies, and in the distance the tops of volcanoes poke above the clouds. The volcanic soil is good for growing crops.

pages.text: All day long, the train stops in small villages. At each stop, you notice the tall spires of mosques (MOSKS), places of worship in the Islamic religion. Most Indonesians are Muslims. Five times a day, you hear the beautiful cries of men calling people to pray.
pages.brief: The train stops in a small village. Above the rooftops rise the tall spires of a mosque, a place of worship in the Islamic religion. Men stand calling people to pray, and their voices carry across the quiet streets.

pages.text: From Java, you take a quick ocean ferry to Bali. Many people on the island live on the slopes of volcanoes. People have carved terraces into the mountainsides that look like huge stair steps. This creates flat fields for growing rice. Hindu temples are everywhere. As Hindus, Balinese people leave food and flowers at temples as offerings to the gods.
pages.brief: A ferry crosses to Bali. On the volcano slopes, mountainsides are carved into terraces that look like huge stair steps, making flat fields for rice. Hindu temples stand everywhere, and Balinese people leave offerings of food and flowers there for the gods.

pages.text: Floating in the Amazon Rainforest Once you leave Indonesia, you fly east along the equator. For hours, you see nothing but the vast Pacific Ocean. Your plane lands in Manaus (mah-NOWS), Brazil, a city located on the Amazon River. As you walk through the old section, you come upon the fish market. It stretches for two city blocks. Thousands of fish—some of them six feet (1.8 m) long—are for sale on rows and rows of tables.
pages.brief: A plane lands in Manaus, Brazil, a city on the Amazon River. In the old section, a visitor walks past a fish market stretching two city blocks. Thousands of fish lie on rows and rows of tables, some of them six feet long.

pages.text: You hop on a boat on a small river that flows into the Amazon. The sounds of the rainforest make a jungle symphony as birds, monkeys, and insects call back and forth. Huge trees, ferns, and vines arch over the water.
pages.brief: A traveller sits in a small boat on a narrow river flowing into the Amazon. Birds, monkeys and insects call back and forth, a jungle symphony of sound. Huge trees, ferns and vines arch over the water.

pages.text: Because the level of the water can rise or fall as much as thirty feet, people build their homes on stilts. The homes are made of wood with roofs made of leaves. There are very few roads in the rainforest because most people live along waterways. You see almost no farms in this region. The forest is too thick, and the soil is too poor. Suddenly, thunder booms, black clouds open up, and a heavy rain falls. After fifteen minutes, the rain stops as suddenly as it began. The steamy heat returns.
pages.brief: Wooden houses with roofs made of leaves stand on tall stilts beside the water, built high because the river can rise or fall thirty feet. Suddenly thunder booms, black clouds open and heavy rain falls; fifteen minutes later it stops and steamy heat returns.

pages.text: Seeing Life on the Congo River Before you leave Manaus, you check the weather in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. You know you are going to need your rain gear. You fly all night across the Atlantic Ocean. When you wake, you are about to land in the capital, Kinshasa. It is located on the Congo River, a long river that drains the rainforest of Central Africa.
pages.brief: A traveller flies all night across the Atlantic Ocean and wakes as the plane comes down over Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The city sits on the Congo River, a long river that drains the rainforest of Central Africa.

pages.text: Wandering the city, you hear an interesting kind of music. You follow the sound and come upon a café. You are told it is ndombolo music, “Afro Pop.” This popular music was invented in the Congo, but it is known throughout the world.
pages.brief: Wandering Kinshasa, a visitor follows an interesting sound and comes upon a café where people are listening to ndombolo music, called Afro Pop — music invented in the Congo and known throughout the world.

pages.text: You are hungry. You ask the waitress for a typical dish. She brings you foufou, a dish made with plantain, yam, or cassava paste rolled into a ball and fried. It is served with either salted fish or barbecued goat meat.
pages.brief: In the café, a hungry traveller asks the waitress for a typical dish. She brings foufou: plantain, yam or cassava paste rolled into a ball and fried, served with salted fish or barbecued goat meat.

pages.text: A Climate Riddle Next stop is Kenya, a country on the east coast of Africa. You leave Nairobi (nye-ROH- bee), the capital, to begin a five-day trip. Starting in the town of Nanyuki, you cross the equator and enter Sirimon Park. All day, you hike through a forest of bamboo, a treelike grass that grows quickly in hot, wet weather. On day two, you enter a treeless area of low grasses. On day three, the land changes again. Now it’s rocky with little plant life. It’s hard to catch your breath and you’re freezing, even though you’re wearing heavy clothes. You think to yourself, “How can this be? I’m on the Equator, but my feet are in snow!” It’s because you are hiking to Mount Kenya, which rises to a height of 17,040 feet (5,194 m)! Do You Know? North or south of the equator, days get longer in summer and shorter in winter. But at the equator, each day (and each night) is very close to twelve hours long, no matter what season of the year it is.
pages.brief: Hikers leave Nanyuki, cross the equator and enter Sirimon Park. Day one is a forest of bamboo; day two, treeless low grasses; day three, rocky ground with little plant life. Freezing and short of breath, they find snow underfoot on Mount Kenya.

pages.text: Reflecting on “Expedition Zero” The equator is a special place that gets lots of sunshine and often lots of rain as well. It is neither north or south. There isn’t much difference between winter, summer, spring, and fall. Traveling the equator, you dripped with sweat in the heat. You had to run for cover in heavy rain. You saw huge rivers draining rainforests. You even saw snow on Mount Kenya. During your journey, you saw many ways of life. Some people in big cities, such as Singapore, live and work in air-conditioned buildings. Others, such as those in the Amazon rainforest, build their homes high above ground in order to stay dry. Expedition Zero showed you that the world is full of variety, even on the same latitude line.
pages.brief: Two ways of life on the equator: in Singapore, people live and work inside air-conditioned buildings; in the Amazon rainforest, families build their homes high above the ground to stay dry. Between them lie heavy rain, strong sunshine and huge rivers draining rainforests.

pages.brief: A steep hillside in a hot, humid tropical climate, cut into wide terraces that look like giant stairs, making flat ground for farming. Warm mist hangs over the slope and the stepped fields follow the curve of the hill.

books.title: Exploring Tide Pools
books.art_why: Tide pools, tides and sea animals are real subjects that can be shown in photographs today.

pages.text: What Are Tide Pools?
pages.brief: A rocky shore at low tide with a shallow pool of seawater held between rocks. Clear water reflects the sky, and wet rocks surround the pool, showing where the tide has pulled back to leave a small pool.

pages.text: What Causes Tides? The tides are caused by the force of gravity. The sun and moon have strong gravity that pulls on Earth. This gravity pulls on both land and water. But only the water can move in response to gravity. When the sun and moon pull on Earth, they pull the ocean water into two mounds.
pages.brief: Earth floats in space with the sun and moon nearby. Their gravity pulls ocean water into two rounded mounds on opposite sides of the planet, while the land stays in place and the water responds to the pull.

pages.text: The rotation, or spin, of Earth causes the rising and falling of the tides. The tides slowly rise and fall as land areas move into and out of where the water is in mounds. There are two high tides and two low tides every 24 hours because Earth makes one rotation each day. The moon also moves around Earth. This movement affects the tides. The moon and sun line up twice each month. They pull on the ocean water together. Their combined gravity causes higher mounds of water, creating the highest and lowest tides of the month. These tides are called spring tides. At other times, the sun and moon pull against each other. Then the high tides are not as high, and the low tides are not as low. These are called neap (neep) tides. Spring Tides Neap Tides.
pages.brief: Earth spins as the moon moves around it, creating two high tides and two low tides in a day. In one view the sun and moon line up and pull together for spring tides; in another they pull against each other for neap tides.

pages.text: The Intertidal Zone.
pages.brief: A rocky shoreline at the edge of the sea, where the water rises and falls with the tides. Wet rocks, shallow pools and exposed shore sit between the high-water line and the low-water line. This is the intertidal zone.

pages.text: What Is Life Like in a Tide Pool?
pages.brief: A shallow rocky tide pool full of life, with clear seawater covering small sea creatures on the rocks. Water surrounds the pool, and the animals are visible in the quiet pool between tides. Some cling to stone; others move slowly through the water.

pages.text: Surviving in the intertidal zone is difficult. Imagine living where seawater washes in and out of your home every day! The animals in tide pools have to deal with waves crashing over them. If they don’t hang on tight or get out of the way, they could be tossed around, battered against rocks, or even swept away. It isn’t just seawater that threatens the animals of the intertidal zone. Exposure to the air and sun is also dangerous. Exposure to air causes two major problems for animals that need to be covered by water. The first problem is drying out. The second problem is exposure to predators. So how do animals in intertidal zones survive?
pages.brief: Waves crash over rocky tide pools while small animals cling tightly to the rocks. Some are left exposed to bright sun and dry air as the tide pulls back. A predator's shadow falls near the pool, and loose animals risk being battered or swept away.

pages.text: Intertidal animals have adapted to life in the tide pools. These animals are used to the tide coming and going from their homes every day. They have ways of clinging to rocks and finding protection from crashing waves. They have ways to keep their bodies from drying out. They also have ways to avoid predators. How a tide pool animal survives depends on whether it can move around. Many animals are attached to the substrate, and they do not move around. This prevents them from being washed away.
pages.brief: Tide-pool animals hold onto rocks and find shelter from crashing waves. Some stay attached to the rock surface and do not move around, while others keep from drying out and avoid predators. Each animal's way of surviving depends on whether it can move.

pages.text: Some animals, such as mussels, have very strong hair-like fibers that attach to the substrate. Other animals, such as barnacles (BAR-nick-els), create hard “glue” to attach themselves to rocks. These animals cannot escape from the sun, air, or predators because they cannot move around. Tide pool animals that are mobile can move around. They are able to run, swim, and crawl. Some of these are sea creatures that become trapped in tide pools during low tide. They cannot return to the sea until the high tide returns. But they can seek shelter from the air, sun, and predators because they are mobile.
pages.brief: Mussels grip rocks with strong hair-like fibers, while barnacles stick fast with hard glue. Nearby, a mobile sea creature crawls through a shallow pool, able to seek shelter from sun, air and predators instead of staying fixed in place like the attached animals.

pages.text: Drying Out Most stationary tide pool creatures have ways to protect their bodies from drying out. Some animals, such as barnacles and oysters, have hard shells. They can close or crawl into their shells during low tide. There they have enough moisture to keep from drying out until high tide returns. The stationary animals most in danger of drying out are the ones with soft bodies such as sea anemones (ah-NEM-oh-nees). These animals are usually found close to the ocean, where the low tide does not uncover them for very long. When the tide is out, they close up their bodies as much as possible to keep from drying out.
pages.brief: Barnacles and oysters close their hard shells on exposed rocks during low tide, keeping moisture inside. Close by, a soft-bodied sea anemone near the ocean closes its body as much as possible, protecting itself from drying out until the high tide returns.

pages.text: Mobile tide pool animals have a better chance of survival. They can move to prevent drying out in the sun and air. Many can dig into the sand. Others seek shelter under rocks or seaweed. A group of very thin crabs called slider crabs can slide their flat bodies into cracks between rocks. Slow animals such as marine snails can hide inside their shells. They can close a little “trap door” to seal themselves inside. But usually there is enough water in a tide pool for mobile animals to swim or crawl about.
pages.brief: A slider crab slides its flat body into a crack between rocks. A marine snail hides inside its shell and closes a small trap door. Nearby mobile animals dig into sand or shelter under seaweed, while enough water remains in the pool for them to swim and crawl.

pages.text: Eating and Being Eaten Eating and being eaten are facts of life everywhere. Tide pool animals have special and interesting ways of finding and eating food. Oysters and clams use hair-like parts to trap tiny animals floating in the water. Anemones and jellyfish sting tiny animals with their tentacles. An octopus uses its strong arms and suction cups to catch other animals. Crabs and lobsters use their claws to pick up food.
pages.brief: Oysters and clams trap tiny animals with hair-like parts. Anemones and jellyfish sting small prey with tentacles, an octopus catches animals with strong arms and suction cups, and crabs and lobsters pick up food with their claws in a busy tide pool.

pages.text: Tide pool animals also have amazing ways to avoid being eaten. Often, the way animals avoid drying out also helps them avoid being eaten. They simply slide under rocks or slip into their shells. Other tide pool animals run, scuttle, swim, or jump to escape. Some tide pool animals blend in with their surroundings. This helps them hide from predators.
pages.brief: A tide-pool animal slides under a rock, another slips into its shell, and small creatures run, scuttle, swim or jump away. One animal blends closely with the rocks and seaweed around it, making it hard for a predator to see.

pages.text: What Lives in Tide Pools? Invertebrates The most common kinds of animals in tide pools are called invertebrates. These animals have soft bodies and no backbones. They range from sponges and corals to octopuses and sea stars. Invertebrates also include anemones, jellyfish, worms, crabs, shrimp, snails, and urchins. Invertebrates can be stationary or mobile. These drawings show invertebrates commonly found in tide pools. Sponges Flat worms Segmented worms.
pages.brief: Soft-bodied invertebrates without backbones fill a shallow tide pool. Sponges, flatworms and segmented worms rest among rocks and seaweed, while other tide-pool invertebrates such as sea stars, anemones, jellyfish, crabs, shrimp, snails and urchins appear nearby in the water.

pages.text: Hard skeletons or shells Soft bodies with tentacles Stationary Bell- or dome-shaped bodies Long tentacles with stinging cells Mobile Anemones Flower-shaped bodies Tentacles with stinging cells Usually, but not always, stationary Sea stars, sea urchins, and sand dollars__ Spiny skin Bodies with sections arranged in a circle Can move slowly.
pages.brief: Sea anemones with flower-shaped bodies and stinging tentacles stand in the pool, usually staying still. Sea stars, sea urchins and sand dollars show spiny skin and bodies arranged in a circle, moving slowly over rocks and sand in the shallow water.

pages.text: Snails and slugs Soft bodies Crawl on single “foot” Octopuses Soft bodies Hard beaks Eight arms Swim very fast Clams and oysters Soft bodies Hard, two-sided shells Usually stationary, but can move in an emergency.
pages.brief: Snails and slugs crawl on a single soft foot. An octopus shows eight arms and a hard beak as it swims fast through the pool. Clams and oysters have soft bodies inside hard, two-sided shells, usually staying still but able to move in an emergency.

pages.text: Barnacles____ Shrimp, crabs, and lobsters.
pages.brief: Barnacles cover a rock near the water, while shrimp, crabs and lobsters move through a rocky tide pool. The barnacles stay fixed to the stone, and the shrimp, crab and lobster are shown together in the shallow seawater around them.

pages.text: Fish Another group of animals commonly found in tide pools is fish. Fish have backbones. Many types of fish are adapted to life in tide pools. Since tide pools are small, fish that live in them are usually small. Other fish get trapped in tide pools when the tide goes out. These fish are not used to living in such a small space. They wait until the tide returns to swim into the open sea.
pages.brief: Small fish with backbones swim in a shallow tide pool. Nearby, other fish trapped by the outgoing tide wait in the small pool, unable to swim into the open sea until the high tide returns and reconnects them to deeper water.

pages.text: Land Animals Many land animals also visit tide pools. The shallow water in tide pools makes it easy for these animals to find and eat sea creatures. Many birds, including seagulls and ravens, eat oysters, mussels, and fish. Mammals such as raccoons and monkeys can scoop up animals and eat them. Plantlike Organisms There are also many plantlike organisms in tide pools. Most of these belong to a group called marine algae. They are also known as seaweed. There are many different types of seaweed, but only some of them are found in tide pools. Seaweed provides good hiding places for animals. It also provides a substrate to which some animals attach themselves or their eggs.
pages.brief: A seagull and a raven stand in shallow tide-pool water eating oysters, mussels and fish. A raccoon and a monkey scoop up sea creatures nearby. Clumps of seaweed provide hiding places and a surface where some animals attach themselves or their eggs.

pages.text: Exploring Tide Pools Tide pools are fun to explore. They are like an aquarium full of sea creatures. The best places to find tide pools are rocky shores. Pay attention to the rise and fall of the tides. Usually newspapers near the oceans show the times and heights of the tides. Remember, the lower the tide, the more you are likely to see. There are things you can do to help you see more creatures in a tide pool. It is best to move slowly and gently to avoid stepping on or crushing animals.
pages.brief: A person walks slowly and gently on a rocky shore at low tide, looking into a tide pool like an aquarium. The low water exposes more of the pool, and a newspaper nearby shows tide times and heights.

pages.text: It is a good idea to pause and look closely at one small area that you find interesting. The longer you look, the more likely you are to see things. Remember that the tide pool is home to many creatures. If you lift up a rock to look for creatures, do it gently. Always put rocks back where you found them. Check with an adult if you want to pick up a tide pool animal. Some of them can sting! Put some water in your hand first to keep the animal moist. And always put sea creatures back where you found them. Animals need to stay in their tide pool homes. They don’t make good pets and are likely to die if they are removed from the tide pool.
pages.brief: A child kneels beside a tide pool and pauses to look closely at one small area, with an adult nearby. The child gently lifts a rock and holds seawater in a hand, keeping a tide-pool animal moist before putting it back where it was found.

books.title: An Apple a Day
books.art_why: Modern food, kitchens, schools, and exercise are real-world today, so photos fit.

pages.text: A Snack, Anyone? If you lived long, long ago, a snack might have been nuts and seeds that you found in the forest. You might have picked wild berries and mushrooms. You might even have munched on an insect. Now many people get food from cabinets, refrigerators, or even vending machines. They might grab fruit, bread, cheese, or even soda and candy. There are so many choices. That’s why the study of food, known as nutrition, is more important than ever.
pages.brief: Split scene: on one side a child in a forest long ago holds nuts, seeds, wild berries, and mushrooms; on the other side a modern kitchen with open cabinet, refrigerator, and vending machine, and a child choosing fruit, bread, cheese, soda, and candy.

pages.text: Try This! How many meals might you eat in your life? 2 Multiply: 3 meals a day times 365 days a year times 90 years Wow! That’s a lot! Nutrients A nutrient is any substance your body needs to live, stay healthy, and grow. The nutrients you need come from what you eat and drink. This is why it is very important to eat foods that contain the right kinds of nutrients. On the next few pages, you will find out about different kinds of nutrients. You will learn what they do for your body and what foods contain them.
pages.brief: A child at a kitchen table with breakfast, lunch, and dinner plates, imagining a long row of meals stretching far into the distance; beside the plates are a glass of water and a mixed plate of foods that supply nutrients for living, staying healthy, and growing.

pages.text: What Is a Protein? Proteins make up the building blocks of your body. They help build and repair cells. Proteins are especially important for strong muscles. Foods that contain protein include meat, fish, eggs, dairy products, beans, nuts, and some grains.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of a strong arm and muscle fibers beside a kitchen table spread with meat, fish, eggs, dairy products, beans, nuts, and grains; small building-block shapes show proteins repairing cells and building strong muscles.

pages.text: What Is a Carbohydrate? Carbohydrates are the nutrients your body uses to make energy. One type is called complex carbohydrates. These give you energy over a long period of time. These are found in foods such as vegetables, many fruits, oatmeal, whole grains, and whole-grain bread. Sugars make up another type of carbohydrates. Sugars create an energy flood followed by an energy crash. This is stressful for your body. These carbohydrates include the sugars in candy and the starches in cakes, cookies, white potatoes, bagels, and many breads. Do You Know? Type 2 diabetes is a disease in which the body can’t manage the amount of sugar in the blood. A history of diabetes in a family can increase the risk of developing the disease. Poor eating habits, including eating too many sweets, can also increase the risk. In some countries, including the United States, type 2 diabetes is increasing.
pages.brief: Split scene: one side shows vegetables, fruit, oatmeal, whole grains, and whole-grain bread giving steady energy; the other shows candy, cake, cookies, white potatoes, bagels, and bread causing a quick energy flood and crash, with a tired child; a family silhouette hints at family history.

pages.text: What Is a Fat? Another nutrient your body needs is fat. Fats are needed for building cells, absorbing certain vitamins, and storing extra energy. Fats occur as animal fats in meat and cheese and vegetable fats in olive oil, nuts, and seeds. Some fats are better for you than others. Vegetable fats from nuts and seeds are better than animal fats from meat and butter. Fats called trans fats are found in pre-made foods such as snacks, cheese products, fried foods, and desserts. They are often called “hydrogenated” or “partially hydrogenated” oils. Studies have shown that these fats are not good for the body.
pages.brief: A plate divided into animal fats such as meat and cheese and vegetable fats such as olive oil, nuts, and seeds; nearby a tray of pre-made snacks, cheese products, fried foods, and desserts; a cutaway cell shows fat being stored and vitamins being absorbed.

pages.text: Vitamins, Minerals, and Water Other nutrients include special chemicals called vitamins. Vitamins help control how your cells use energy. They help your body build the chemicals it needs to see, digest food, and fight diseases. Your body also needs nutrients called minerals. Minerals help your bones, blood, and other parts grow and function. Minerals also help your brain and nerves send signals to your body. Many people get the vitamins and minerals they need from pills called supplements. Water is also necessary. It helps you digest food by carrying nutrients to all the cells in your body. It is found in many foods, such as fruits, vegetables, meats, and even bread. But you should also drink six to eight glasses of water each day. Taking water breaks during a long hike is a good idea.
pages.brief: A hiker taking a water break on a trail, with a bottle and six to eight glasses of water nearby; around them are fruits, vegetables, meat, bread, and a small bottle of supplement pills, plus a cutaway body showing vitamins, minerals, bones, blood, brain, and nerves.

pages.text: Calories A calorie is a bit of energy that you get from food. Calories provide the fuel that allows our bodies to do work. It’s important to eat enough food each day to give your body the energy it needs. The number of calories a person needs depends on many things. These include their age, body type, and how active they are. For example, an athlete needs many more calories than an average person. Taking in too few or too many calories compared to how active we are can lead to health problems.
pages.brief: A calorie as a small spark of energy fueling a child running and playing; beside them an athlete bicycling hard and an average person sitting quietly; a simple balance scale shows too few and too many calories leading to health problems.

pages.text: Activities and Calories Health experts say children and teens should exercise for at least sixty minutes a day. That doesn’t have to happen all at once, however. Here are some examples of how many calories a 150-pound adult burns on average doing various activities: Watching TV 43 calories per hour Cleaning the house 115 calories per hour Playing table tennis 171 calories per hour Bicycling 174 calories per hour Walking 198 calories per hour Washing a car 193 calories per hour Swimming 288 calories per hour Playing basketball 450 calories per hour Jogging 654 calories per hour.
pages.brief: A 150-pound adult shown in a row of activities: watching television, cleaning the house, playing table tennis, bicycling, walking, washing a car, swimming, playing basketball, and jogging, with a sense of different energy amounts for each activity.

pages.text: Smart Eating There are many different opinions about what foods people should eat. But many people agree that some foods are better for your health than others. Be sure to eat protein, complex carbohydrates, healthy fats, and lots of colorful vegetables and fruits every day. Eating a balanced diet is a good way to stay healthy. Get to know which kinds of foods you like from each of these groups. Try different kinds of proteins, grains, vegetables, and fruits. And remember that if a snack food comes ready to eat from a bag or box you probably shouldn’t eat much of it.
pages.brief: A colorful balanced plate with protein, complex carbohydrates, healthy fats, and many vegetables and fruits; a child choosing different foods from each group; nearby an open snack bag and box, with only a small portion taken from them.

pages.text: PROTEIN Eat more: fish, chicken, turkey, eggs, lean meat (without much fat), low-fat dairy Eat less: meat with lots of fat or with breading; fried and deep-fried meats; highly processed meats like lunchmeat; high-fat dairy CARBOHYDRATES Eat more: colorful vegetables and fruit, oatmeal, brown rice, whole grains, whole-grain bread, whole-grain pasta Eat less: sugar, white bread, cakes, white potatoes, white flour pasta FATS Eat more: nuts, most vegetable oils, fish oil Eat less: saturated fat (the fat in meat and dairy products) Avoid: trans fats (found in processed foods) WATER Drink a lot!
pages.brief: Four food areas: protein foods like fish, chicken, eggs, lean meat, and low-fat dairy; carbohydrates like vegetables, fruit, oatmeal, brown rice, and whole-grain bread; fats like nuts, vegetable oils, and fish oil; and a large glass of water, with smaller piles of fried meats, processed lunchmeat, high-fat dairy, sugar, cakes, white potatoes, and trans fats set aside.

pages.text: Some recipes contain foods from each of the main food groups. Can you match each food above to the right group?
pages.brief: A kitchen counter spread with a pepper, pineapple, sausage, pizza crust, tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, mushrooms, walnuts, and an onion; a child's hands sort the foods into groups beside a pizza recipe, showing ingredients from each main food group.

pages.text: Nutrition Facts Look at a box of cereal, a snack bar wrapper, or a bottle of juice. You will probably see a Nutrition Facts chart. The chart shows what kinds of nutrients are in the food. The first lines of the chart tell you the serving size. That is the amount of the food you should eat at one meal or snack. It might surprise you to see that a container of food contains two or more servings. Suppose a bag of chips contains two servings. If you eat the whole bag, you’re eating two servings. That means you’re getting double the calories and nutrients shown in the chart.
pages.brief: A cereal box, a snack bar wrapper, and a bottle of juice on a kitchen counter; a close-up shows a nutrition panel with serving size and nutrient amounts; a bag of chips is opened beside two stacked serving bowls to show two servings in one container.

pages.text: The calories are listed below the serving size. This jar of sauce has 70 calories in one serving. The nutrients are listed under the heading “Amount Per Serving.” The chart divides fats into saturated and unsaturated. Saturated fats are less healthy. Carbohydrates are divided into fiber and sugars. Sugars are less healthy. Most nutrition facts also list all the ingredients in order from most to least. For example, this jar of sauce is made mostly of tomato puree and tomatoes. It has just a little lemon juice.
pages.brief: A jar of tomato sauce on a kitchen counter with a close-up of its nutrition panel and ingredient list; nearby fresh tomatoes, tomato puree, and a lemon show the sauce is mostly tomato with just a little lemon juice; small sections compare saturated and unsaturated fats and fiber and sugars.

pages.text: Healthy Habits The adults in your life probably make many of your food choices. You may have someone in your life who prepares your breakfast and dinner. You may eat lunch in the school cafeteria. Even your soccer coach or your scout leader may provide snacks for your practices and meetings.
pages.brief: A child at home with an adult preparing breakfast and dinner; at school the child eats lunch in a cafeteria; on a soccer field a coach hands out snacks; at a scout meeting a leader provides snacks for the group.

pages.text: As you get older, you will have more chances to choose what you eat. Knowing about the types of nutrients will help you stay healthy. You will also need to think about calories. Begin to follow healthy habits now. Eat well, exercise, and drink plenty of water. Food can feed your health and happiness!
pages.brief: An older child choosing foods at a table, with a plate of healthy food, a water bottle, and running shoes nearby; the child looks forward to more food choices, healthy habits, exercise, and plenty of water, with a bright, happy expression.

pages.text: Try This!  Smart Eating You can use the Smart Eating section of this book to plan your meals for a day. Be sure to include healthy foods from each of the three main food groups. If you eat something unhealthy, try to eat something healthy at the same meal. Or have healthy foods at another meal that day. And remember to eat a good breakfast each morning. You’ll have energy all day, and you’ll do better in school. Breakfast Morning Snack Lunch Afternoon Snack Dinner Bedtime Snack.
pages.brief: A child planning a day of meals on a table with breakfast, morning snack, lunch, afternoon snack, dinner, and bedtime snack plates arranged in a row; each plate includes healthy foods from the three main food groups, with a good breakfast first and a happy, energetic child ready for school.

books.title: Jane Goodall
books.art_why: Jane Goodall is a real person, and photographs of her, the chimpanzees, and Gombe exist.

pages.text: The Watcher Jane Goodall was born in England in 1934. As a child, she liked to learn about animals and watch how they behaved. Jane loved to read colorful stories about wild animals that lived in Africa. She even dreamed about living there. Jane was sure that, one day, she wanted to work with animals and write stories about them.
pages.brief: Young Jane Goodall sits in an English home, reading colorful storybooks about wild African animals. In her imagination, a lush African landscape opens around her with wild animals moving among trees. She looks curious and happy, already watching and learning about the creatures she loves and hopes to study one day.

pages.text: Off to Africa At age eighteen, Goodall graduated from high school and became a secretary. She wondered how being a secretary would get her to Africa, but she kept working. By 1957, Goodall had saved enough money to take a trip to Kenya, in eastern Africa. Within months, she met a famous scientist named Dr. Louis Leakey. Dr. Leakey was studying how apes and humans were alike and different.
pages.brief: At eighteen, Jane Goodall works as a secretary, typing at a desk with papers nearby. Later, she travels toward Kenya, carrying a suitcase and savings from her job. In eastern Africa, she meets the scientist Dr. Louis Leakey, who studies how apes and humans are alike and different.

pages.text: At the time, Dr. Leakey needed a new assistant. Even though Goodall had no scientific training, he hired her for the job. She learned fast and loved the work. One day, Leakey talked about starting a special field study of chimpanzees. In a field study, scientists live near the animal they want to learn about. For this special study, Dr. Leakey needed someone who was patient and curious. The person would have to feel comfortable living in the forest among the chimps. He asked Goodall. For her, it was a dream come true.
pages.brief: Dr. Louis Leakey asks Jane Goodall to become his assistant, even though she has no scientific training. She learns quickly and loves the work. He describes a special field study of chimpanzees, needing someone patient, curious, and comfortable in the forest. Jane looks eager and delighted when he asks her to take on the study.

pages.text: Into the Forest Goodall was twenty-six years old in 1960. That year, she went to the Gombe (GOME-bay) Forest in Tanzania, where the chimpanzees lived. At Gombe, Goodall sat quietly on a hill, watching the chimpanzees all day, every day—even in the rain. Goodall took careful notes. She noticed that the chimps always stayed in family groups. So she gave each chimp in each family group a name that began with the same letter of the alphabet.
pages.brief: In 1960, twenty-six-year-old Jane Goodall sits quietly on a hill in Gombe Forest, Tanzania, watching chimpanzees all day. Rain falls around her, and she takes careful notes. Below her, chimpanzees stay close in family groups. She gives each chimp a name that begins with the same letter as its family group.

pages.text: The Gombe Gang For a long time, the chimps were afraid of her. Then a curious older chimp that Goodall had named David Greybeard came to her camp in search of food. She hid a banana under her shirt and let him find it. As his trust in her grew, he led Goodall into the forest to meet his family. The chimp family let her sit and watch them on a daily basis. Her reports about her early observations of the family group upset many long-held scientific beliefs about chimps. The Woman Who Named Things Some scientists doubted Goodall’s findings. They didn’t believe that chimps had feelings or intelligence. They certainly didn’t think a serious scientist should give personal names to the animals she studied.
pages.brief: David Greybeard, an older chimpanzee, comes into Jane Goodall's camp looking for food. Jane hides a banana under her shirt and lets him find it. The chimp's trust grows, and he leads her into the forest to meet his family, where she sits and watches them.

pages.text: At the time, people believed that chimps ate only plants. Goodall saw David Greybeard’s family eat meat. Later, she saw him poke a stick into a termite mound. He pulled it out—and ate a termite snack. Goodall realized two things. One, David had used a tool to get food. Two, he had first stripped the leaves off the stick so it would fit in the small hole. In other words, he had also made a tool. Her shocking report caused scientific debate. It also won her important support and funding.
pages.brief: David Greybeard pokes a stripped stick into a termite mound while Jane Goodall watches closely. He pulls the stick out and eats a termite. His family eats meat, not only plants. Jane records how he made and used a tool, a discovery that caused scientific debate and brought her important support and funding.

pages.text: Thanks to David Greybeard, the other chimps also came to trust Goodall. She was able to watch complete life cycles—from birth to death. She saw and reported behavior that no researcher had ever observed before.
pages.brief: Thanks to David Greybeard, other chimpanzees trust Jane Goodall. She sits near them in the forest and watches complete life cycles, from a mother caring for a newborn to an elderly chimp. She observes behavior no researcher has seen before and writes reports about the chimpanzee families living around her.

pages.text: Goodall stated that each chimp had its own personality, just like humans. She found that chimps showed a whole range of emotions. They were happy, sad, angry, loving, and jealous. She saw them hold hands, laugh, and throw tantrums. Over many years, Goodall’s discoveries and reports gave the world new ideas about chimpanzees. Her work made many scientists reconsider what makes humans different from other animals.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall watches chimpanzees show many emotions. Two chimps hold hands, others laugh and play, while one throws a tantrum. She sees them happy, sad, angry, loving, and jealous, each with its own personality. Her observations make scientists reconsider what makes humans different from other animals.

pages.text: Trouble in the Forest In time, Goodall began to see a dark future for her Gombe chimpanzees. Many people in this part of Africa are very poor. Some were cutting down the chimps’ forest in order to build houses or grow crops there instead. Some were using the trees for firewood. Chimps also faced danger from hunters. Some hunters were stealing baby chimps and selling them to zoos, circuses, and even as pets. Most grown-up chimps don’t make good house pets, however.
pages.brief: In the forest around Gombe, people cut down trees for houses, crops, and firewood. A hunter carries a stolen baby chimpanzee, while adult chimps remain in the disappearing forest. The chimpanzees face danger from hunters who sell babies to zoos, circuses, and as pets, though grown chimps do not make good house pets.

pages.text: Goodall realized that if these practices continued, the Gombe chimpanzees were in danger of dying out completely. She decided that she would have to leave Gombe and her chimps in order to save them. Goodall began to travel the world. She talked with important groups about her work. She asked for help to save both the chimps and the forests they need in order to survive.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall leaves Gombe Forest with a suitcase, choosing to travel the world to save the chimpanzees. She speaks to important groups of people, showing them her work and asking for help. Behind her, the forest and its chimpanzees remain in danger of dying out unless their habitat is protected.

pages.text: The Work Goes On Jane Goodall once left behind everything she knew to live among and learn about another species. More than sixty years have passed since she first went to the Gombe Forest, but the work she started there continues. Jane Goodall died on October 1, 2025, at the age of ninety-one. She will be remembered for her work to protect chimps and preserve their habitats. Her research changed the way that people view all animals.
pages.brief: An older Jane Goodall stands quietly in the Gombe Forest with chimpanzees nearby, her notebook in hand. The forest stretches around her, a lasting home for the chimps she studied and protected. More than sixty years after she first arrived, the work she began continues, changing how people view animals.

pages.text: Goodall visits a chimp rescue center in Uganda in 2018. Jane Goodall Programs Sadly, chimp numbers in Gombe and much of Africa continue to drop. The work to protect them continues, however. In 1977, Goodall began the Jane Goodall Institute This institute gives money to scientists who study chimps in the wild. It also teaches people living near wild places how to help protect the wildlife in their area. In 1991, Goodall began Roots & Shoots The Roots & Shoots program began in Tanzania with just twelve local teens. Today, it operates in more than 130 countries and has thousands of members. Its main goal is to educate young people about problems that exist right around them. To learn more, go to: www.rootsandshoots.org and www.janegoodall.org.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall visits a chimpanzee rescue center in Uganda in 2018, standing near rescued chimps. Nearby, a small group of local teenagers works together on a wildlife project. This connects to the Roots & Shoots program, which began in Tanzania with twelve teens and now educates young people about problems in their own communities.

books.title: Edible Bugs
books.art_why: Edible insects, farms, markets and dishes are real-world subjects that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Good-For-You Foods People around the world have been eating insects for thousands of years. The thought of eating them makes some people squirm. However, insects are good for people’s health. They are full of the nutrients people need.
pages.brief: A spread of edible insects — grasshoppers, crickets and larvae — arranged on a clean plate beside fresh vegetables, showing insects as a healthy food. People's hands reach for them, suggesting people around the world eating insects for their nutrients.

pages.text: Insects have large amounts of protein. For example, 100 grams of grasshoppers have around 20 grams of protein. That’s only 6 grams of protein less than the same amount of beef, and far less fat. Termites and some caterpillars are also great sources of iron. Crickets are high in calcium. Other insects, such as termite and ant queens, have large amounts of healthy calories. Nutrition Information Animal Calcium (mg) Protein (g) Fat (g) Iron (mg)
pages.brief: A nutrition comparison scene: a pile of grasshoppers next to a cut of beef on a table, with small bowls of crickets and termites nearby, illustrating protein, iron, calcium and calorie content of different insects and meat.

pages.text: Crickets or Cows? Eating insects is also good for the planet. To feed a growing human population, global farming has to expand. Yet farming for billions of people greatly harms the planet. One cause of this is a demand for beef. Raising cows hurts the planet in several ways. Cows give off a greenhouse gas that helps cause global warming. A cattle ranch creates about ten times more harmful waste than a large insect farm. Also, insect waste is a great fertilizer and good for the soil.
pages.brief: A large cattle ranch with cows grazing in a dusty field, and beside it a compact insect farm with stacked trays of crickets, showing the difference in waste and harm to the planet between the two kinds of farming.

pages.text: Much of the world’s farmland is used to raise and feed cows. Insect farms take up far less space. They also need much less food to provide the same amount of nutrients. Most cows today eat grain, which needs large amounts of land and water to grow. In some parts of the world, farmers clear more trees each year to make room for cattle. This destroys homes for thousands of species already at risk. The best way to save these forests may be to offer people insect protein.
pages.brief: An aerial view of wide farmland and cleared forest where cattle graze, with a small insect farm building nearby, showing how much land and water cows need compared with insects.

pages.text: Popular Bugs and Ways to Eat Them There are more than 2,000 edible insects around the world. People eat them in all sorts of ways. In Thailand, some outdoor stands sell crispy, fried water bugs. People add sauce just as others might put mustard or ketchup on a hot dog. Other people snack on grasshoppers and bamboo worms.
pages.brief: A busy outdoor street market in Thailand with a vendor at a stand selling crispy fried water bugs, a customer adding sauce to a paper tray, and other snacks of grasshoppers and bamboo worms on display.

pages.text: Sushi and Snails Food culture changes. There was a time when Italians thought tomatoes were poisonous. Americans once disliked lobster and fed it to prisoners. Few cultures ate raw fish fifty years ago. Now sushi is popular all over the globe. In French restaurants, snails are a popular appetizer. The dish is called escargot (es-car-GO), the French word for “snail.” The snails are taken out of their shells, cooked, and placed back inside the shells. Diners use special tools to pull out the snail meat. Water bugs boiled in a special sauce can be found in some restaurants in China. The bugs and sauce are served over rice. When the weather gets chilly, some people have a steaming bowl of ant soup.
pages.brief: A restaurant table showing a plate of sushi, a dish of cooked escargot in shells with special tools, a bowl of water bugs over rice, and a steaming bowl of ant soup, illustrating changing food cultures.

pages.text: One town in Brazil cooks queen ants every October and November. This is when queen ants come out from hiding underground. People collect the ants and remove their wings. Some fry the ants. Others dip them in chocolate. The people say queen ants have a minty taste. Edible Arthropods Most arthropod species are insects. Lobsters, crabs, spiders, scorpions, and many other animals are also arthropods. These animals all have their skeletons on the outside of their bodies. The tasty meat is on the inside. Some outer shells can be eaten, too.
pages.brief: In a Brazilian town, people collect queen ants emerging from the ground, remove their wings, and fry or dip them in chocolate, while a nearby diagram-like display shows a lobster, crab, spider and scorpion as arthropods with outside skeletons.

pages.text: In Mexico, some people enjoy French-fried caterpillars or ant eggs covered in butter. For dessert, chocolate-covered locusts or candy-covered worms are sweet treats. Central Africa has a wide range of edible insects. In Ghana, many people fry or roast termites. They can also be ground into flour for baking.
pages.brief: A table of Mexican treats: French-fried caterpillars, ant eggs covered in butter, chocolate-covered locusts and candy-covered worms, with a bowl of fried termites and termite flour in Ghana shown alongside.

pages.text: Some Australians munch on witchetty grubs, which look like large white caterpillars. These insects have crisp skin and a smooth filling that tastes like nuts. Some restaurants in Japan serve fried silk moth cocoons. Fried grasshoppers and other insects are sold in some stores.
pages.brief: An Australian scene of witchetty grubs, large white caterpillars, on a plate, next to a Japanese restaurant plate of fried silk moth cocoons and a store shelf selling fried grasshoppers.

pages.text: Be Careful! Never eat wild insects! It’s very important to remember that. Walking into your backyard for a buggy snack can be dangerous. Insects that live outside can be covered with stuff that might harm you if you eat it. Also, some insects are poisonous and can make you very sick.
pages.brief: A cautionary backyard scene: wild insects on leaves and grass, with a child's hand reaching toward a bug, showing that outdoor insects may be covered with harmful substances or be poisonous.

pages.text: People who cook and eat insects should be careful to buy them from farms. Farmed insects have special diets. They don’t contain things that might harm people. In the United States, the best way to find edible insects is on the Internet. People can find live insects, meals made with insects, and tasty insect recipes.
pages.brief: A farmed insect facility with clean trays of insects on special diets, and a person at a computer ordering edible insects and insect recipe ingredients online from the United States.

pages.text: Let’s Start Cooking! David George Gordon, a chef from Washington, wrote the Eat-A-Bug Cookbook. People like his pasta with six-legged meatballs, which are made with crickets. Other favorites are fried tarantula and white chocolate and waxworm cookies. Gordon believes that eating insects is a better way to get protein than eating chicken, cows, or pigs. Insects are cheap and easy to farm in plain fish tanks. Raising them does not harm the planet. Insects may just be the food of the future.
pages.brief: Chef David George Gordon in a Washington kitchen holding his Eat-A-Bug Cookbook, with plates of pasta and six-legged cricket meatballs, fried tarantula, and white chocolate and waxworm cookies, plus fish tanks where insects are farmed.

books.title: The Force of Water
books.art_why: Real-world rivers, landforms, water, and people can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Water, Earth’s most important resource, is a mighty force. It covers most of Earth and is always at work changing Earth’s surface. Plants, animals, and humans need water to survive. So, we have to take care of the water for the good of the Earth.
pages.brief: A wide view of Earth with oceans and land, water moving across the surface and changing it. Plants, animals, and people are shown depending on water to live, and people are caring for the water for the good of the Earth.

pages.text: Water is found above ground in lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, and oceans. It is also found below ground, between rocks and sand. This water is called groundwater. The air also holds water as clouds and an invisible gas called water vapor.
pages.brief: Lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, and oceans appear above ground while groundwater sits between rocks and sand below. Clouds drift in the air, and water is also held in the air as an invisible gas called water vapor.

pages.text: Water on the Move Much of Earth’s water is on the move. Water falls from clouds as rain and snow and drains into streams and rivers. The land surrounding streams and rivers is called a watershed. Streams flow into small rivers, and small rivers flow into bigger rivers. The smaller streams and rivers that flow into bigger rivers are called tributaries. Over time, much of the water that flows into streams and rivers reaches the oceans.
pages.brief: Rain and snow fall from clouds and drain into streams and rivers. The land around the streams and rivers forms a watershed, with smaller streams and tributaries flowing into small rivers and then bigger rivers, and the water moving over time toward the ocean.

pages.text: UNITED STATES GULF OF MEXICO.
pages.brief: A broad view shows the United States and the Gulf of Mexico, with the large land area of the United States stretching beside the wide gulf waters and a long coastline where the land and water meet along the gulf.

pages.text: Water as a Force As water flows in rivers and streams, it picks up dirt, sand, and rocks. The dirt and sand carried by water are called sediment. Sediment helps water carve away the land. The Grand Canyon is one of Earth’s largest canyons. Over millions of years, it was carved by the fast-moving Colorado River. It shows how powerful water can be.
pages.brief: Fast-moving river water picks up dirt, sand, and rocks as sediment. The sediment helps the water carve away land, and the Grand Canyon appears as a huge canyon cut by the fast-moving Colorado River over millions of years.

pages.text: When water slows down, the sediment settles to the bottom of the stream or river. Deposits of sediment form new land, called sandbars and deltas. Large deltas form where big rivers meet oceans.
pages.brief: As river water slows, dirt and sand settle to the bottom of the stream or river. Deposits of sediment build new land called sandbars and deltas, and a large delta forms where a big river meets the ocean.

pages.text: Flooding Sometimes massive amounts of rain and snow fall to Earth, causing streams and rivers to spill over their banks. The land around the streams and rivers floods when this happens. Flooding can cause lots of damage.
pages.brief: Heavy rain and snow fall to Earth, making streams and rivers rise and spill over their banks. The land around the streams and rivers is flooded, and the floodwater causes lots of damage to the area.

pages.text: When the water recedes to the riverbed, the dirt carried by the floodwater is left on land. Over the years, this dirt forms a floodplain. The soil of a floodplain is rich in nutrients from the river. Crops grow well in floodplains, but can be ruined when water floods the area again.
pages.brief: After floodwater recedes to the riverbed, dirt carried by the flood is left on the land. Over the years this dirt forms a floodplain, where soil rich in nutrients helps crops grow well, though crops can be ruined when water floods again.

pages.text: Water Is Important Rivers and streams have many uses besides carving land. People use rivers for swimming, boating, and fishing. People also have used rivers for thousands of years to transport goods from place to place. Today, large barges and ships move cargo over rivers. Lumber companies move logs from forests to mills over rivers.
pages.brief: People swim, boat, and fish in rivers and streams. People have used rivers for thousands of years to transport goods, and today large barges and ships carry cargo while a lumber company moves logs from a forest to a mill by river.

pages.text: Factories use millions of gallons of water each year to make the things people use. We use water in our homes to clean and cook. How else do you use water in your home? Dams built on rivers use the force of water to make electricity. Farms use water to irrigate crops.
pages.brief: Factories use millions of gallons of water to make things people use, and water is used in homes to clean and cook. A dam uses the force of river water to make electricity, and a farm uses water to irrigate crops.

pages.text: Streams and rivers are home to many living things. People and other animals depend on streams and rivers for drinking water. Some industries and large cities dump their waste into rivers, and this waste pollutes the water. Polluted water is harmful to humans, plants, and other animals that live in the water or use it to stay alive.
pages.brief: Streams and rivers are home to many living things, and people and other animals depend on them for drinking water. Waste dumped into a river by industries and large cities pollutes the water, which is harmful to humans, plants, and animals that live in or use the water.

pages.text: The World’s Rivers Nile, North Africa 6,677 km (4,150 mi) Amazon, South America 6,280 km (3,900 mi) Yangtze, China 6,115 km (3,800 mi) Mississippi, United States 3,780 km (2,350 mi) Volga, Russia 3,740 km (2,325 mi) Mackenzie, Canada 1,802 km (1,120 mi) River Dee, UK 110 km (70 mi) Conclusion The force of water running in rivers and streams changes the shape of the land in many ways. Rivers and streams are important to humans, other animals, and plants. Rivers and streams will take care of us as long as we take care of them.
pages.brief: A world view shows the Nile in North Africa, the Amazon in South America, the Yangtze in China, the Mississippi in the United States, the Volga in Russia, the Mackenzie in Canada, and the River Dee in the UK. Rivers and streams change the land and are important to humans, animals, and plants.

books.title: China
books.art_why: A country book about real places and people today, not a biography of a named person.

pages.text: China Where Is It? The People’s Republic of China is one of the largest countries in the world, along with Russia, Canada, and the United States. Russia and China cover a large part of the continent of Asia. In fact, China is almost as large as the entire continent of Europe. Many countries border China, including India, Mongolia, Russia, and North Korea. To the east of China are the Pacific Ocean, the South China Sea, and the East China Sea. China has about 14,500 kilometers (9,000 mi.) of coastline.
pages.brief: A globe view of Asia shows China as one of the largest countries, with Russia covering much of the same continent. China’s borders meet India, Mongolia, Russia and North Korea, while its long eastern coastline touches the Pacific Ocean, South China Sea and East China Sea.

pages.text: The Forbidden City in Beijing was built in the early 1400s. It first housed the emperor’s family in 1420. China has several large cities, including Shanghai, Beijing, and Hong Kong. Beijing, the capital, is located in northeast China. Its name has changed many times, yet Beijing is one of the oldest cities in the world. It is over three thousand years old. More than fifteen million people live there today. Beijing is a mixture of both ancient and modern buildings. Skyscrapers reach for the sky beside buildings that have stood for hundreds of years. At the center of Beijing is the Forbidden City. This palace was built in the fifteenth century. It was the home of China’s emperors for more than five hundred years. It is called the Forbidden City because only the emperor of China could enter every area in it. Today, the palace is a museum.
pages.brief: In Beijing, tall skyscrapers stand beside buildings that have stood for hundreds of years. At the center is the Forbidden City, a palace built in the fifteenth century and home to emperors for over five hundred years. The palace is a museum today.

pages.text: People More than 1.3 billion people live in China. That is more people than in any other country. The United States has about 316 million people. That’s about one quarter the size of China’s population. A village in China More than half of the people in China live in towns, villages, or the countryside. People who live in rural regions often grow crops and raise livestock for food. Meanwhile, people who live in towns and villages may manufacture goods as well as perform other jobs.
