Many people also live in large cities, which are centers for trade and business. Many different ethnic groups live in China. The Han is the largest group. Other groups include the Hui (HWAY), Zhuang (JWAHNG), Dai (DY), Yao (YOW), Miao (MEOW), Tibetans (teh-BET-uhns), Manchus (MAN-chooz), and Mongolians (mahn-GOH-lee-uhns). Most Chinese people speak Mandarin, which means “common language.” People in China also speak many other languages, including Cantonese and English.
pages.brief: A rural Chinese village shows people growing crops and raising livestock for food. Nearby, people in a town manufacture goods, while a large city is busy with trade and business. A diverse group of Chinese people, including Han and other ethnic groups, speak Mandarin and other languages.

pages.text: It can take years to master the art of calligraphy. Every line or dot must be perfectly spaced, showing balance and beauty. Chinese writing does not use the letters of the English alphabet. Instead, it uses thousands of characters that stand for words or parts of words. Some of these characters look like what they mean. For example, the character for the word forest looks like three trees in a forest. Chinese artists have been creating amazing works for thousands of years. One of the more interesting art forms is calligraphy, which is a combination of art and writing. Calligraphers use ink to create beautiful Chinese characters. The characters combine to create stunning images as well as powerful poetry. Mandarin Characters Here are the Mandarin characters for some words. fire mountain forest woman.
pages.brief: A calligrapher uses ink to create Chinese characters, combining art and writing. The characters form stunning images and powerful poetry, with careful spacing and balance. One character for forest looks like three trees; other Mandarin characters include fire, mountain, forest and woman.

pages.text: China’s Landforms Land Because China is so large, it has many different landforms. Deserts, mountains, and canyons stretch across the northwest region. This area also includes one of the lowest places on Earth. It is a salt lake located in the Turfan Depression. The lake is 154 meters (505 ft.) below sea level. In the southwest, several mountain ranges reach up into the sky. The most famous range is the Himalayas. This range includes the highest mountain in the world, Mount Everest. The southwest also includes high plateaus.
pages.brief: In northwest China, deserts, mountains and canyons stretch across the land. A salt lake in the Turfan Depression lies 154 meters below sea level. In the southwest, the Himalayan mountain range rises high, including Mount Everest, the world’s highest mountain, and high plateaus.

pages.text: Tian Shan (tsee-EN SHAHN) Mountains Bamboo forest Yellow River In the east, the land includes flat plains, wetlands, and forests. This flat land is the only land suited to farming. Part of the Yangtze (yank-SEE) River flows through this region, as well as part of the Yellow River. These rivers help provide water for the fields. Farmers grow rice, wheat, potatoes, and peanuts. Other crops include tea, barley, and cotton. In addition, many people across China raise animals, such as chickens, goats, pigs, sheep, and cattle.
pages.brief: In eastern China, flat plains, wetlands and forests cover the land. Parts of the Yangtze River and Yellow River flow through this farming region, providing water for fields. Farmers grow rice, wheat, potatoes and peanuts, along with tea, barley and cotton, and raise chickens, goats, pigs, sheep and cattle.

pages.text: History Experts estimate that Chinese civilization began over five thousand years ago! In fact, some of the oldest artifacts in the world have been found in China. Ancient Chinese people kept good records, which have helped experts learn about the country’s history. The ancient Chinese named their land Zhongguo (JOONG-gwah), which means “the Middle Kingdom.” They believed that it was the center of the civilized world. In order to protect the land from invaders from Mongolia, the Chinese emperor began building a giant wall. Work began around 220 bc and continued for nearly 2,000 years. The Great Wall is actually a series of walls in northern China and southern Mongolia. One of the sections stretches for about 8,850 kilometers (5,500 mi.). For more than three thousand years, parts of China were ruled by emperors. Sometimes one family would rule an area for hundreds of years. This was known as a dynasty. Under these dynasties, China became an advanced civilization. Great Wall of China.
pages.brief: Ancient artifacts and records show China’s long history. The Great Wall stretches across northern China and southern Mongolia, a series of walls begun around 220 bc to protect the land from invaders. For thousands of years, emperors and dynasties ruled parts of China, helping it become an advanced civilization.

pages.text: Confucius Kong Fuzi (KOHNG FOO-tsu), also known as Confucius (kuhn-FYOO- shuhs), was a Chinese philosopher and teacher. Confucius believed that people, including government leaders, should serve others. He also believed that all people had the right to an education. Confucius died in 479 bc, but his teachings are still followed today. The ancient Chinese people discovered and invented many things we still use today. They were the first to create paper, nearly two thousand years ago. They also invented the magnetic compass, which helped sailors find their way. Gunpowder is another Chinese invention. They used it to blast rocks apart and make fireworks for celebrations. The ancient Chinese were also the first to make fabric from silk. It became the country’s most popular export for many years. People traveled from around the world on a trade route called the Silk Road to get it. The fibers used to make silk come from the cocoons of silkworms. The ancient Chinese discovered they could separate the fibers from the cocoon. Then, they spun the fibers together to make a strong thread. The thread was woven together to make beautiful cloth.
pages.brief: Confucius, a Chinese philosopher and teacher, taught that people and government leaders should serve others and that all people have the right to an education. His teachings are still followed today, and ancient Chinese inventions include paper, a magnetic compass, gunpowder, and silk made from silkworm cocoons.

pages.text: The Chinese New Year celebration lasts two weeks and includes dances such as this fire dragon dance. Celebrations One of the most widely celebrated holidays in China is the New Year. The Chinese New Year takes place in late January or early February, depending on the Chinese calendar. During the festival, dancers carry colorful dragons or lions through the streets. People light firecrackers and enjoy feasts. They decorate their doorways with poetry written on strips of red paper. These traditions are thought to bring good luck in the coming year. The Lantern Festival is another popular celebration in China. Held soon after the Chinese New Year, it celebrates the first full moon of the year. People hang colorful paper lanterns outside with riddles attached. Others try to solve the riddles to receive a small gift. People also enjoy sweet dumplings made of rice flour.
pages.brief: During Chinese New Year, dancers carry colorful dragons and lions through the streets while people light firecrackers, enjoy feasts, and decorate doorways with poetry on red paper. Later, the Lantern Festival celebrates the first full moon with colorful paper lanterns, riddles, small gifts, and sweet rice-flour dumplings.

pages.text: Dumplings are popular in many areas of China. They are filled with meat or vegetables. Food Rice is the basis for many meals in China. Other common ingredients are noodles, potatoes, meat, fish, and tofu. The typical meals can be different depending on the region. In some parts of China, the food may be very spicy. In the southeast near the ocean, seafood is a main part of many dishes. In the north, many people use wheat instead of rice. For dessert, many Chinese people have seasonal fruit. They may also enjoy candies, pancakes, or a dish made of shaved ice and fruit called baobing (BOU-beeng).
pages.brief: A table of Chinese food shows rice-based meals with noodles, potatoes, meat, fish and tofu. In the southeast near the ocean, seafood is common; in the north, wheat replaces rice; in some regions food is spicy. Dumplings filled with meat or vegetables are popular, and dessert may be fruit, candy, pancakes or baobing.

pages.text: Every year, millions of people visit the Great Wall of China. It is considered by many Chinese people to be the country’s national symbol. Conclusion China’s history stretches back thousands of years. Its diverse people have created interesting and unique cultures. Stretching across much of Asia, its wonders include breathtaking mountains, the Great Wall, delicious food, and exciting celebrations. If you visited China, which wonder would you want to experience first?
pages.brief: Many visitors walk along the Great Wall of China, which many Chinese people consider the country’s national symbol. The scene looks out over mountains and the long wall stretching across Asia, representing China’s long history, diverse people, delicious food and exciting celebrations.

books.title: India
books.art_why: The book includes maps and historical scenes best shown with drawn illustrations.

pages.text: India Afghanistan China Bhutan Pakistan New Delhi Nepal India Bangladesh Myanmar (Burma) Mumbai ARABIAN SEA Bay of Bengal ASIA Andaman INDIAN OCEAN Sri Lanka Nicobar Where Is It? India is a country in Asia that is mainly a peninsula. Along the northern edge of India are the countries of Pakistan, China, Nepal (nuh-PAHL), and Bhutan (boo-TAHN). To the east are Bangladesh (bahng-gluh-DESH) and Myanmar (mee-AHN-mar). Just south of India is the island of Sri Lanka (SHREE LAHNG- kuh). To the southwest of India is the Arabian Sea. To the southeast is the Bay of Bengal. India also includes some groups of islands.
pages.brief: A broad view of India as a peninsula in Asia, with the northern countries of Pakistan, China, Nepal, and Bhutan, and Bangladesh and Myanmar to the east. Sri Lanka sits just south, the Arabian Sea lies southwest, and the Bay of Bengal southeast, with island groups offshore.

pages.text: The capital of India is New Delhi (DEL-ee), which is part of the larger city of Delhi. The two areas are very different. Delhi is a very old city, but New Delhi was built in the 1920s and 1930s. Delhi is a complex maze of small streets crowded with small shops, while New Delhi has wide streets and modern shopping centers. More than twenty million people live in Delhi and New Delhi combined.
pages.brief: New Delhi, the capital area within the larger city of Delhi, shown with wide modern streets and shopping centers beside the older, crowded Delhi lanes of small shops. More than twenty million people live across the combined city, with busy streets and many buildings.

pages.text: People More than one billion people live in India. Only China has more people. Most Indian people live in the countryside, even though India does have some large cities. Most homes in the rural areas don’t have running water. People must go to a well and bring home water every day. About half of the people in rural areas don’t have electricity, either. Half of the people in India make their living growing crops, mainly grains. They also raise cattle, water buffalo, and other animals. However, most Indian people do not raise cattle to eat, because many religions in India, including Hinduism, believe cows are sacred. They use cattle for plowing their fields and for transportation. They raise sheep, goats, and chickens for meat. The Taj Mahal The Taj Mahal (TAHZH muh- HAHL) is one of the most well-known landmarks in India. It was built by the emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal after she died. It took forced laborers twenty-two years to complete the Taj Mahal.
pages.brief: Rural Indian people fetch water from a well and work with grain crops and animals, using cattle to plow fields and for transportation. In another view, the Taj Mahal stands as a well-known landmark, built by Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal after she died.

pages.text: Most Indian cities are extremely crowded. Many people live in apartment buildings along very narrow streets. Because India has such a large population, it has been hard for the country’s electricity supply to keep up with the demand. In some Indian cities, it’s very common for the power to go out. The center of Hindi language filmmaking is Mumbai (mum-BY). It was once known as Bombay because the British pronounced Mumbai incorrectly. Mumbai releases more than a thousand movies per year. It is called Bollywood locally and globally. The Bollywood audience is global, as well.
pages.brief: Crowded Indian city streets with many people living in apartment buildings along narrow lanes. Power outages are common in some cities. In Mumbai, the center of Hindi filmmaking once called Bombay, more than a thousand movies are released each year for a global Bollywood audience.

pages.text: India’s Landforms India Land The Himalayas (him-uh-LAY-uhz) form India’s northern border. They are the highest mountains in the world and cut off India from the rest of Asia. This is why India is sometimes called a subcontinent. A low-lying plain stretches across northern India. This rich land was formed long ago as rivers flooded and left soil behind. The Thar Desert is in western India.
pages.brief: The Himalayas rise as India's northern border, the highest mountains in the world, cutting India off from the rest of Asia. A low-lying plain stretches across northern India, formed by river floods leaving rich soil. The Thar Desert lies in western India.

pages.text: The Ganges (GAN-jeez) and Indus Rivers lie in the northern plains of India. For Hindus, the Ganges is a sacred river. Hindus from all over India travel to the river to enter its waters. South of the Indus and Ganges Rivers lies raised land that takes up more than half of India. In May or June every year, winds bring rain as they blow northward from the Indian Ocean. This is the monsoon season. During this time, rain falls almost every day in the afternoon. Most of India’s rain falls during this hot, wet season.
pages.brief: The Ganges and Indus Rivers flow through India's northern plains. Hindus travel to the sacred Ganges to enter its waters. South of the rivers lies raised land covering more than half of India. Monsoon winds bring rain from the Indian Ocean in May or June, with afternoon rain almost every day.

pages.text: Celebrations People in India celebrate many special days. Diwali (dee-VAH-lee) is a festival that lasts for five days. During this time, people across religions light small candles. They shoot firecrackers and give sweets and other gifts to friends and family. Holi (HOH-lee) is a spring Hindu celebration known as the festival of colors. Today, people of all religions celebrate Holi to mark the end of winter. They throw colored water and powder on each other. Children use water guns filled with colored water to spray colors on their friends. People also sing, dance, and enjoy special foods and drinks.
pages.brief: People across India celebrate Diwali for five days by lighting small candles, shooting firecrackers, and giving sweets and gifts to friends and family. For Holi, the spring festival of colors, people of all religions throw colored water and powder, and children spray friends with colored water from water guns while singing and dancing.

pages.text: History India’s civilization is very old. About 2,300 years ago, people living in the land now known as India had been mostly united under one ruler. About 1,300 years ago Muslims set up a kingdom with Delhi at its center. Muslim rule lasted until the 1600s. Europeans had landed in India as early as 1498. That’s when Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama (VAHS-koh DAH GAH-mah) sailed to India. By 1858, Great Britain had taken control of the country. In the 1920s, a lawyer named Mohandas Gandhi (moh-huhn- DAHS GAHN-dee) joined the movement to resist British rule. He asked them to protest British rule in nonviolent, or peaceful, ways. By 1947, India was free. Since gaining independence, India has faced many obstacles but continues to grow. India elected its first woman prime minister, Indira Gandhi, in 1966. Forty-one years later, in 2007, it elected its first woman president.
pages.brief: A historical scene of India's long civilization: Vasco da Gama sailing to India in 1498, Muslim rule centered on Delhi, and British control by 1858. Mohandas Gandhi leads a peaceful protest against British rule, and India becomes free in 1947; Indira Gandhi later becomes prime minister.

pages.text: Animals India’s wildlife includes many exciting species. India is the only country in the world with both lions and tigers. It is also the home of two kinds of leopards. The snow leopard of the Himalayas is very rare. One of India’s most famous reptiles is the cobra. The Indian cobra hunts small animals, such as rats and mice. It has been known to bite humans because its prey often lives in towns and villages.
pages.brief: Indian wildlife: lions and tigers both live in India, along with two kinds of leopards, including the rare snow leopard of the Himalayas. The Indian cobra hunts small animals such as rats and mice and has been known to bite humans because its prey often lives in towns and villages.

pages.text: The Indian elephant is very strong. People once used it to lift logs in India’s forests. They also used it to carry crops and people. Some people still use the elephant to help them with their work. Today, wild Indian elephants are found in most parts of India. They are endangered, though, because of the loss of their habitat. Near the Bay of Bengal, the mangrove forests provide a special habitat for sea turtles, sharks, and crocodiles. This saltwater swamp is also the largest home of Bengal tigers in the world. A male Bengal tiger can grow to 3 meters (10 ft.) in length. It can weigh as much as 230 kilograms (500 lbs.). The tigers often swim in the swamp waters to catch prey.
pages.brief: A strong Indian elephant carries logs, crops, or people, helping with work in India's forests; wild Indian elephants are endangered because their habitat is being lost. Near the Bay of Bengal, mangrove forests shelter sea turtles, sharks, and crocodiles, and are the largest home of Bengal tigers, which often swim in the swamp waters to catch prey.

pages.text: Conclusion India has a long history. It also has a very large, diverse population. It’s a country trying to find a balance between caring for its people and maintaining its natural beauty. Fascinating animals and interesting people make India a unique country with much to learn about.
pages.brief: A concluding view of India as a unique country with much to learn about, showing its long history, large and diverse population, and natural beauty. People and fascinating animals appear together, suggesting the country's effort to balance caring for its people with maintaining its natural beauty.

pages.text: India Population: 1.4 billion Land: 2,973,193 sq km (1,147,956 sq. mi.) Capital City: New Delhi Primary Language: Hindi Primary Religion: Hinduism Currency: Rupee (ROO-pee)
pages.brief: India's key facts shown together: a population of 1.4 billion, a land area of 2,973,193 square kilometers, New Delhi as the capital city, Hindi as the primary language, Hinduism as the primary religion, and the rupee as the currency.

books.title: Incredible Places to Stay
books.art_why: The hotels and locations are real places that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Incredible Places to Stay.
pages.brief: A dramatic cover-style view of extraordinary hotels in faraway places suggests adventure and travel. Unusual places to spend the night appear around the world, inviting readers to imagine a journey to remarkable destinations and to wonder what each incredible stay might be like.

pages.text: World Map of Incredible Hotels 3 INDIAN OCEAN 5 Sala Silvermine Hotel, Sala, Sweden 6 Marina Bay Sands Hotel, Marina Bay, Singapore 7 Jules’ Undersea Lodge, Key Largo, Florida 8 Tundra Lodge, Manitoba, Canada 1 Skylodge Adventure Suites, Cuzco, Peru 2 Hôtel de Glace, Quebec, Canada 3 Giraffe Manor, Nairobi, Kenya 4 Treehotel, Harads, Sweden Introduction Get ready to go on a tour of some of the world’s most unusual and amazing hotels. You’ll spend nights on four continents. You’ll swim to the bottom of the sea, sleep in a cave, and meet endangered animals. As different as these hotels are, they all share one thing: each offers you an incredible experience. Pack your bags and let’s go!
pages.brief: A world map shows the far-flung locations of unusual hotels on four continents. Small hotel illustrations are placed across the globe, and a packed bag suggests the start of a tour: swimming to the sea bottom, sleeping in a cave, and meeting endangered animals.

pages.text: Sky High The first stop on your tour is Skylodge Adventure Suites in the Sacred Valley of Cuzco, Peru. Getting to Skylodge is not easy! You will need to hike up a mountain or ride zip lines just to get to your room. Once you reach the top, you can sleep in a see-through capsule hanging high above the valley floor. Each capsule is solar powered and has a 300-degree view of Sacred Valley. You will eat dinner and breakfast in a see-through capsule, too, and you can watch the birds above you. You’ll feel just like you’re in a giant bird nest!
pages.brief: In the Sacred Valley of Cuzco, Peru, a hiker climbs a mountain and rides a zip line toward a see-through capsule hanging high above the valley floor. Inside, a guest enjoys a 300-degree view while birds fly above; dinner and breakfast are set in another clear capsule.

pages.text: A Cool Place to Stay From Cuzco, you’ll travel to the Hôtel de Glace (O-tel DEH GLAHS). It is a cool hotel located just a few minutes outside of Quebec City, Canada. How cool is it? It’s a work of art made of ice! The rooms, halls, and most of the furniture are carved out of ice. Artists and workers spend about forty days every winter building the hotel because it all melts away in warm weather.
pages.brief: Just outside Quebec City, Canada, artists and workers carve an entire hotel from ice, shaping rooms, halls, and most of the furniture. The cool structure gleams like a work of art in winter, built over about forty days because it will melt away when warm weather returns.

pages.text: You’ll need to wear your heavy winter clothes during your stay. The temperature in the hotel is only 23° to 27°F (–5° to –3°C). It’s as cold as a freezer in there! You’ll sleep in a special extra-warm sleeping bag because the beds are made out of thick slabs of ice.
pages.brief: Inside the ice hotel, a guest wears heavy winter clothes in a freezer-cold room. The temperature is only 23° to 27°F. A thick slab of ice forms the bed, and the guest settles into a special extra-warm sleeping bag for the night.

pages.text: Breakfast with Giraffes The next stop on your tour is Nairobi, Kenya. There, at Giraffe Manor, you will share breakfast with some very special guests. The forests around Giraffe Manor are home to Rothschild’s giraffes. These giraffes are some of the tallest in the world. Adults can measure up to 20 feet (6 m) from their hooves to the tops of their heads.
pages.brief: At Giraffe Manor in Nairobi, Kenya, guests sit down to breakfast with Rothschild’s giraffes. The tall giraffes stand near the hotel, surrounded by forest; adults can reach up to 20 feet from hooves to the tops of their heads.

pages.text: Every morning, the giraffes leave the forest and visit the hotel. They stick their heads through open windows and doors. Guests feed them pellets made from dry grass, corn, and molasses. Giraffe Manor is more than a nice hotel. Profits from the hotel go to a local wildlife conservation center.
pages.brief: Every morning at Giraffe Manor, giraffes leave the forest and poke their heads through open windows and doors. Guests feed them pellets made from dry grass, corn, and molasses. The friendly visit shows how the hotel supports a local wildlife conservation center.

pages.text: In the Trees From Kenya, you’ll travel to Harads, in northern Sweden. There you’ll find the Treehotel—a hotel made up of strange tree houses. During your visit, you will stay in one of six separate tree-house rooms. The rooms hang 14 to 20 feet (4 to 6 m) off the ground. Each of the tree-house rooms is unique, but three of them are extra special. The outside of one of these rooms, the Mirrorcube, is covered with glass that reflects the woods around it. The glass makes the room nearly invisible.
pages.brief: In Harads, northern Sweden, six separate tree-house rooms hang 14 to 20 feet off the ground among the trees. One room, the Mirrorcube, is covered in glass that reflects the surrounding woods, making the room nearly invisible.

pages.text: The Bird’s Nest tree house is completely covered in a tangle of tree branches. It looks like the home of an enormous bird. The UFO is a strange room built to look like a flying saucer. The UFO has outside landing lights and a ladder that you can bring inside at night. It looks as though an alien has come to Earth for a vacation.
pages.brief: The Bird’s Nest tree house is wrapped in a tangle of branches, looking like the home of an enormous bird. Nearby, the UFO room is built to look like a flying saucer, with outside landing lights and a ladder that can be pulled inside at night, as if an alien has come to Earth for a vacation.

pages.text: While you’re in Sweden, you can stop in the town of Sala. There you’ll find the deepest hotel room in the world. The Sala Silvermine Hotel sits on top of a closed silver mine. The mine’s tunnels are more than 12 miles (19 km) long and 980 feet (300 m) deep. That’s as deep as the Eiffel Tower is tall! Most of the rooms in the hotel are near the mine’s opening. However, if you want a really special experience, you can spend a night hundreds of feet underground.
pages.brief: In Sala, Sweden, the Sala Silvermine Hotel sits above a closed silver mine with tunnels more than 12 miles long and 980 feet deep. Most rooms are near the mine’s opening, but a special experience waits hundreds of feet underground.

pages.text: The Mine Suite is located more than 500 feet (152 m) beneath the surface. A special guide will lead you down to a room with a bed and chairs, a bathroom, and snacks. Dress in warm clothes. The temperature in the mine itself is only about 28°F (–2°C), but the room is warmed to 64°F (18°C). Wowser! Take a dip in the world’s largest rooftop swimming pool at the Marina Bay Sands Hotel in Singapore. While swimming in a pool that is almost 500 feet (152 m) long, visitors can admire city views from 650 feet (198 m) aboveground!
pages.brief: Deep underground, a guide leads a guest to the Mine Suite more than 500 feet beneath the surface, with a bed, chairs, bathroom, and snacks; the mine is cold, but the room is warmed. Aboveground in Singapore, swimmers admire city views from a huge rooftop pool at Marina Bay Sands Hotel.

pages.text: Sleeping with Fish The last stop on your tour is Jules’ Undersea Lodge in Key Largo, Florida. Be prepared to get wet! The lodge is 21 feet (6 m) underwater, resting at the bottom of the Largo Sound lagoon. You’ll need scuba gear to get to your room. The lodge includes two bedrooms and a common room. You can find snacks and breakfast in the common room. For dinner, you can even order pizza. A staff member from the hotel will happily swim it down to you in a watertight box!
pages.brief: At Jules’ Undersea Lodge in Key Largo, Florida, a guest in scuba gear swims down 21 feet to a lodge resting on the bottom of the Largo Sound lagoon. Inside are two bedrooms and a common room; a staff member swims dinner pizza down in a watertight box.

pages.text: Conclusion From the forests of Kenya to the bottom of the sea, amazing hotels are everywhere. These incredible places to stay offer you far more than just a bed for the night. They offer you experiences that you’ll never forget! Polar Bear Fun Tundra Lodge in Manitoba, Canada, looks like a train on huge wheels. The entire hotel moves over snow so that guests can get very close to polar bears.
pages.brief: Amazing hotels appear from Kenya’s forests to the sea floor, offering unforgettable experiences rather than just a bed for the night. In Manitoba, Canada, the Tundra Lodge looks like a train on huge wheels; the whole hotel moves over snow so guests can get very close to polar bears.

books.title: Nature Stinks!
books.art_why: All subjects are real plants, animals, and natural phenomena that can be photographed.

pages.text: Nature Stinks!
pages.brief: A playful introductory nature scene suggests a bad smell in the air, with a simple outdoor setting and a sense of surprise. No people, animals, plants, or objects are specified on this page, so keep the image open and atmospheric, with no words or labels.

pages.text: Stinky Nature If you’ve ever smelled a skunk, you know it is not a pleasant odor. In fact, it’s terrible! Did you know that both plants and animals can smell bad? Stinky plants usually smell bad to attract insects that help them reproduce. Animals give off odors to attract mates and keep other animals away. Whether plant or animal, nature’s smelliest living things use odors to help them survive.
pages.brief: A skunk stands in a natural setting, releasing a terrible odor that drifts through the air. Nearby, a stinky plant attracts insects, while other animals use odors to attract mates or keep enemies away, showing how smells help living things survive.

pages.text: Stinky Furry Animals Skunks are probably the most famous smelly animals. They use their odor to keep enemies away. When an enemy gets near, a skunk growls and stomps its feet. If that doesn’t frighten the enemy away, look out! The skunk lifts its tail and sprays a terrible-smelling liquid. The liquid shoots out from the area near the base of its tail. Striped polecats may smell even worse than their skunk cousins. A striped polecat’s spray can cause burning pain.
pages.brief: A skunk growls and stomps its feet as an enemy approaches in a natural setting. The skunk lifts its tail and sprays terrible-smelling liquid from the base of its tail. Beside it, a striped polecat is shown, its spray causing burning pain.

pages.text: Skunks and striped polecats aren’t the only stinky furry animals. The lesser anteater is four times stinkier than a skunk! It, too, shoots a smelly liquid from the area near the base of its tail. Then there’s the opossum. An opossum will pretend to be dead if an enemy is near. This is called “playing possum.” It stays still and releases stinky green slime.
pages.brief: A lesser anteater stands in a natural setting, shooting a smelly liquid from near the base of its tail. Nearby, an opossum plays possum by staying completely still with an enemy close by, releasing stinky green slime as it pretends to be dead.

pages.text: A smelly liquid marks the spot where a wolverine has been. A wolverine, or “nasty cat,” also pees on saved food before hiding it. The smell helps the wolverine find the food later and discourages other animals from eating it.
pages.brief: A wolverine, also called a nasty cat, moves through a natural setting and leaves a smelly liquid mark where it has been. The wolverine pees on saved food before hiding it; the smell helps it find the food later and discourages other animals from eating it.

pages.text: The release of scent can be a warning as well. Male musk oxen fight each other to mate with females. Males use their stinky urine as a signal. It warns other males to keep their distance. The urine sticks to their long belly hair and makes them smell terrible.
pages.brief: Two male musk oxen fight each other in a natural setting, competing to mate with females. Their stinky urine acts as a signal warning other males to keep their distance, and the urine sticks to their long belly hair, making them smell terrible.

pages.text: Stinky Plants The corpse flower is the world’s smelliest flower. This plant smells like rotting flesh. The plant’s disgusting smell attracts flies and beetles that eat rotting animals. These insect visitors don’t find the food they’re looking for, but they pick up pollen. When the insects visit other corpse flowers, they spread the pollen and help corpse flowers reproduce. These flowers also produce their own heat and steam to help their odor spread far and wide. The stinking root parasite doesn’t smell like rotting flesh— it smells like poop! This African plant’s unpleasant smell comes from inside its flowers. The smell brings dung beetles, which pollinate it. (Dung is another word for poop. Dung beetles love dung!)
pages.brief: A corpse flower blooms in a natural setting, giving off a smell like rotting flesh that attracts flies and beetles. The flower produces heat and steam to spread its odor. Nearby, a stinking root parasite from Africa shows its flowers, whose poop-like smell brings dung beetles that pollinate it.

pages.text: Stinky Birds The hoatzin (wat-SEEN) is the real name for the “stinkbird.” This bird mainly consumes leaves. The food breaks down in the bird’s crop (the area under its throat) before reaching its stomach. This way of eating makes the hoatzin smell awful.
pages.brief: A hoatzin, the bird called the stinkbird, sits in a natural setting eating leaves. The leaves break down in its crop, the area under its throat, before reaching its stomach. This way of eating makes the hoatzin smell awful.

pages.text: Vultures are used to bad odors. After all, their diet consists of the stinky flesh of dead animals. When an enemy is near, vultures throw up! The stuff they vomit is extra nasty. It contains rotten meat and stomach acid strong enough to cause burns.
pages.brief: A vulture stands near the stinky flesh of a dead animal in a natural setting. When an enemy comes near, the vulture throws up extra-nasty vomit containing rotten meat and stomach acid strong enough to cause burns.

pages.text: Stinky Bugs Some bugs also use odor to stay safe. The bombardier beetle can’t fly to escape its enemies, so it has a strong weapon. It can release a hot cloud of stinky, deadly spray. It’s hot enough to kill many enemies and burn humans.
pages.brief: A bombardier beetle stands on the ground in a natural setting, unable to fly away from an enemy. It releases a hot cloud of stinky, deadly spray from its body; the spray is hot enough to kill many enemies and burn humans.

pages.text: What millipedes lack in speed, they make up for in stink. Millipedes can’t move fast, so they need a different way to stay safe. If an enemy comes near, they curl up and give off a stinky liquid. Some millipedes even shoot the smelly stuff.
pages.brief: A millipede curls up on the ground in a natural setting as an enemy comes near. Because it cannot move fast, it gives off a stinky liquid to stay safe, and some millipedes even shoot the smelly stuff at enemies.

pages.text: Other Stinky Animals The common musk turtle has another name—stinkpot! It smells bad when other animals disturb it. A stinky yellow liquid comes out of the back of its body. The mink frog uses scent to keep enemies away as well. Its stink has been compared to rotten onions. It gives off this nasty smell to stay safe from other animals.
pages.brief: A common musk turtle, also called a stinkpot, sits in a natural setting. When other animals disturb it, a stinky yellow liquid comes out of the back of its body. Nearby, a mink frog gives off a smell compared to rotten onions to keep enemies away.

pages.text: Protecting the Nest The green woodhoopoe lives in Africa south of the Sahara Desert. The female uses odor to protect her nest. She sprays a dark, stinky liquid to keep enemies away. Good and Stinky Being stinky helps many plants and animals stay alive. For plants, the odor brings insects that help them reproduce. For animals, the odor often helps keep enemies away. It can also help an animal eat food or get mates. Stinky steam, spray, vomit, slime, and urine are some of nature’s smelly ways of helping living things survive.
pages.brief: A female green woodhoopoe in Africa south of the Sahara Desert sprays a dark, stinky liquid to protect her nest from enemies. The scene also suggests how smelly steam, spray, vomit, slime, and urine help plants and animals survive by attracting insects, keeping enemies away, finding food, or getting mates.

books.title: Deep in the Ocean
books.art_why: Real ocean animals, undersea volcanoes, ships and scientists can all be photographed today.

pages.text: Deep Underwater Imagine taking a trip to the deepest part of the ocean. What kinds of things would you expect to see? Would it be dark or light? Would the water be clear or cloudy? Would it be warm or cold? Would you find strange new animals and plants?
pages.brief: A wide view of deep, dark ocean water far below the surface, empty and cold, with only faint shapes fading into blackness. No sunlight reaches here, the water looks cloudy and dim, and no shore or surface can be seen above or below.

pages.text: Sunlight warms the surface, or shallow parts, of the ocean down to about 200 meters (656 ft). Plants and animals that need sunlight and warm water live there, such as dolphins and sharks. Deep in the ocean, other animals, including squid and viperfish, live in water that is cold and dark.
pages.brief: Bright sunlit shallow water near the ocean surface, with dolphins swimming and a shark gliding past. Far below them, in cold dark water, a squid and a viperfish hover in the gloom, showing the warm bright top and the cold black depths.

pages.text: Ocean Zones.
pages.brief: A tall cross-section of the ocean from the bright sunlit surface down through fading blue-green water to a black bottomless depth. Light fades with every meter of depth, showing the warm shallow layer, the dim middle water and the cold dark zone below.

pages.text: Oceanographers Scientists who study the ocean are called oceanographers (oh-shuh-NOG-ruh-furs). They often live for months on a ship and work seven days a week. Some study what a sea animal eats and where it lives. Others study the ocean water itself. All of them have to understand biology and chemistry. Biology is the study of living things. Chemistry is the study of what things are made of.
pages.brief: Oceanographers at work on the deck of a research ship at sea, one lowering equipment over the side while another checks notes. The ship sits on open water under a wide sky, and the scientists wear working clothes, busy with the ocean water and the animals they study.

pages.text: Using Satellites for Tracking Satellites can help to track sea animals’ travels. Scientists tag some animals with electronic sensors. A satellite can track the signal from the tag on the animal’s fin or back. Tracking the signal shows where the animal goes.
pages.brief: A sea animal swimming in open water with a small electronic sensor tag attached to its fin, while high above, a satellite circles the Earth. The satellite sends a signal down toward the tagged animal, showing how its travels can be tracked across the ocean.

pages.text: Counting the Sea Animals What types of animals live in the ocean? Where do they live? How many are there? Oceanographers studied and counted animals for ten years to learn the answers. They looked at all the world’s oceans from the North Pole to the South Pole. The surprising report is called the Census of Marine Life. Released in 2010, it contains information from more than 540 different groups of researchers.
pages.brief: Many different sea animals spread through the world's oceans, from icy polar water to warm tropical seas, with researchers on ships counting them. Nets, cameras and notebooks are in use as the oceanographers work through every ocean from the North Pole to the South Pole.

pages.text: The Census of Marine Life The first surprise was where things lived: everywhere —in all water levels and temperatures! Marine species lived in the hottest and coldest places in the oceans. Some species lived in deep places without light or oxygen. Another surprise was how many new species were discovered. More than twelve hundred new marine species have been described.
pages.brief: A crowded spread of marine life in every kind of water: animals in steaming hot vents, in freezing polar seas and in pitch-black depths without light. Strange new species are shown alongside familiar ones, all discovered in oceans around the world.

pages.text: Living in Hot and Cold Water The very cold Deep Ocean Zone has hot volcanoes in it. The water temperature at a volcano can be 400°C (752°F), which is hot enough to melt lead. Some species of shrimp, crabs, worms, and bacteria live in this very hot water. These animals use sulfur to live rather than sunlight.
pages.brief: Deep down on the ocean floor, hot volcanic vents pour out shimmering water at 400 degrees, hot enough to melt lead. Shrimp, crabs, worms and clumps of bacteria crowd around the scalding vents in the cold dark Deep Ocean Zone.

pages.text: Huge groups of Arctic sea life were also found living in freezing water. Some species of squid, cod, and jellyfish live under solid ice that is 700 meters (2,296 ft) thick. Many of these species slow down their movements to save energy so they don’t freeze.
pages.brief: Under a thick ceiling of solid Arctic ice, squid, cod and jellyfish drift in freezing water, moving slowly. The ice above is vast and heavy, and the animals hang almost still in the bitter cold, saving their energy so they do not freeze.

pages.text: What Did We Learn? Scientists learned that life is even more adaptable than they had originally thought. Animals living in the deep ocean have found ways to survive in harsh environments. These environments are places where it would be impossible for most other species to survive. The marine census counted more than 230,000 species. More than 6,000 new species had never been seen before! Some creatures were see-through. Some had warning lights that turned on and off. Others had long feelers instead of eyes. Some had teeth so long that they overlapped their jaws. Some made their own antifreeze to stay warm.
pages.brief: A gallery of deep-ocean survivors: a see-through creature, one with glowing warning lights switched on, another with long feelers instead of eyes, one with teeth crossing its jaw, all in dark water. They live where most other species could never survive.

pages.text: What else lives in the deep ocean? Scientists keep finding new species and new facts. The more they look, the more they find. They think that only one-fourth of all marine life has been counted. Only some of those species have even been described yet. There are many more surprises to come! Explore More To learn more about the Census of Marine Life, go to its website at www.coml.org. Each week, new discoveries are added to the marine census project map at www.comlmaps.org/ census-on-google-earth. On the Internet, search terms such as deep sea species, blind lobster, or NASA oceanography.
pages.brief: A scientist in a small submarine shining a light on a never-seen animal in deep black water, while others on a ship above record the find. New species keep appearing out of the dark, and much of the ocean still waits to be explored.

books.title: Awesome Ants
books.art_why: Text includes prehistoric ants and body parts best shown by drawings.

pages.text: A Little History You’ve seen them marching through grass and across sidewalks. You may have even seen them crawling over your kitchen counter or inviting themselves to your picnic. They come in colors such as red, yellow, brown, and black. We’re talking about ants—tiny, strong, awesome ants.
pages.brief: Ants of red, yellow, brown, and black march through grass, across a sidewalk, over a kitchen counter, and around picnic food. Tiny but strong, they crawl in lines through everyday places where ants appear, showing how easily they make themselves at home.

pages.text: Ants are about 100 million years old, which means they were crawling around under the dinosaurs, early mammals, and ancient birds! Between then and now, they’ve changed a lot. Ants used to look more like wasps with shorter jaws. Today, more than 10,000 species of ants live in deserts, rainforests, swamps, and cities. They live on every continent except Antarctica. They have been able to survive so long because of their bodies and how they live. Through the years, they have been able to adapt to changes in their environments.
pages.brief: Ancient ants crawl beneath dinosaurs, early mammals, and ancient birds. Across a wide landscape, modern ants live in deserts, rainforests, swamps, and cities on every continent except Antarctica. The scene contrasts early wasp-like ants with today’s many species.

pages.text: Body Parts Like all insects, ants have six legs and three body parts. The back part of their body is the abdomen. This part holds the heart and stomachs. Some ants have stingers and poison sacs that they use to protect themselves from predators. Their three pairs of legs attach to the middle part, called the thorax. Each leg has three joints and little hooks that allow ants to climb almost anything. Ants don’t have ears, but they can hear by feeling vibrations through their legs and feet.
pages.brief: A side view of an ant shows six legs and three body parts. The abdomen holds the heart and stomachs, while three pairs of jointed legs with little hooks attach to the thorax. Some ants have stingers and poison sacs; vibrations pass through legs and feet.

pages.text: The head contains the brain, two eyes, antennae, and jaws. The jaws open and close like scissors. They are used for cutting and carrying things and also for digging and hunting. They are an ant’s most important tool. Ants can lift more than twenty times their own weight. Ants also have other mouthparts for chewing food and drinking.
pages.brief: An ant’s head is shown with its brain, two eyes, antennae, and scissor-like jaws. The jaws cut, carry, dig, and hunt, while other mouthparts chew food and drink. The ant’s strength lets it lift more than twenty times its own weight.

pages.text: The two eyes, called compound eyes, are each made up of many smaller eyes. Even though ants have so many eyes, their eyesight is not very good, so they use their antennae to get around. The antennae are like all-in-one sense machines. Ants use them to taste, smell, hear, and communicate with other ants through touch. The long, thin antennae bend in the middle, like a human’s elbow, and are always moving around. Ants don’t have lungs. Instead they breathe through small holes all over their bodies.
pages.brief: An ant’s two compound eyes are made of many smaller eyes, but its eyesight is poor. Long, thin antennae bend in the middle and move constantly as the ant tastes, smells, hears, and touches other ants. Small holes all over its body let it breathe without lungs.

pages.text: Let’s Talk Ants communicate with each other in three ways: touch, sound, and smell. Ants touch each other with their antennae in different ways to send different messages. They can also make noises to communicate by rubbing their legs together or on their bodies. Scientists have learned that these special noises are a call for help.
pages.brief: Two ants touch antennae in different ways to send messages. Another ant rubs its legs together and on its body to make a special noise, a call for help. The scene shows ants communicating by touch and sound.

pages.text: The main way ants communicate is by smell. They release special chemicals, called pheromones (FAIR-oh-mohnz), which other ants can smell long after the first ant is gone. Different smells send different messages. For example, a crushed ant releases chemicals that attract other ants. Some chemicals work as an alarm to warn other ants that danger is nearby. The chemicals also make the other ants attack anything near them that is not an ant from the same colony. An ant that has found food will lay down a trail of chemicals for other ants to follow. The trail allows them to find the food and return to the colony. The more ants that follow the trail, the stronger it gets.
pages.brief: Ants follow a chemical trail left by a nestmate. One ant lays pheromones from food back to the colony, and more ants join, making the trail stronger. A crushed ant releases chemicals that attract others or warn of danger, making nearby ants attack anything not from their colony.

pages.text: One Big, Happy Family Ant colonies, which can have millions of members, are filled with activity. Some ants are active year-round, while others hibernate in the winter. Some ants build their colonies in logs or trees, but most build their colonies underground. Some ants reinforce the entrance to their colony by mixing twigs into the dirt for added protection from flooding. They have many different rooms, which all have different uses. Some rooms store food or eggs, while others are used to care for the young. Colonies even have rooms for ants to relax in and a special chamber for the queen.
pages.brief: An ant colony is busy with millions of members. Most ants build underground, with some in logs or trees. Twigs mixed into the dirt protect the entrance from flooding. Inside, different rooms store food or eggs, care for the young, let ants relax, and hold the queen.

pages.text: Within the colony, every ant has a job and special skills to do that job. Worker ants and soldier ants find food and protect the nest. They are social insects and work together as a group. Worker ants are usually the ones you see above the ground. They are the older ants. Other ants build the nest, take care of the young, and do other jobs. The ants that work inside the nest tend to be younger ants. All these ants are female, but only one is allowed to lay eggs: the queen. In other words, all the ants in a colony are related. What About the Boys? Male ants have only one purpose in most colonies: to mate with the queen. Once they’ve done their duty, most male ants simply die.
pages.brief: Inside and outside a colony, ants do different jobs. Older worker ants and soldier ants find food and protect the nest above ground, while younger ants build, care for the young, and work inside. All are female except the males, whose only purpose is to mate with the queen before they die.

pages.text: The Queen The queen is the leader of the colony, but she doesn’t tell the other ants what to do. The largest of all the ants in the colony, the queen is an egg-laying machine. Some queens can lay thousands of eggs every day. Most colonies have only one queen. When other queen ants hatch, they must fly away and start other colonies. When they start laying eggs, they lose their wings. Queens can also live very long for insects—more than twenty-five years—but when they die, so does the colony. I Can Fly! Like queens, some males can also fly. When they land near a colony, worker ants rip the wings off. Then they rush the male to the queen so the two can mate before the male dies.
pages.brief: The queen, the largest ant in the colony, lays thousands of eggs each day. She does not give orders. New queens fly away to start colonies and lose their wings when they begin laying eggs. A flying male is rushed to the queen by workers after they remove his wings.

pages.text: Let’s Go Floating Not even water can stop some ants. They climb on top of each other and link their legs until they form a raft or bridge made of their own bodies. Yep, Ants Are Awesome Ants may be small, but they can do awesome things. Thousands or millions of ants working together can build bridges to cross a gap in their path. They can also shape themselves into boats to float across rivers safely. As a group, they can overpower animals hundreds of times their own size for food.
pages.brief: Ants climb on top of each other and link their legs to form a raft or bridge made of their own bodies. Thousands or millions work together to bridge a gap, shape themselves into boats to float across a river, and overpower animals hundreds of times their size for food.

pages.text: A trail usually means the ants are moving to a new home—or they’ve found something very tasty. So the next time you come across a trail of ants, stop and watch. Better yet, follow them— just don’t step on their trail. When you see what these little gals are capable of, you’ll understand just how awesome they are.
pages.brief: A long trail of ants crosses the ground, heading toward a new home or something tasty they have found. The trail invites a close look at the tiny ants, showing what these little workers can do together when they follow it.

books.title: Jack-o'-Lanterns
books.art_why: The book mixes modern jack-o'-lanterns with legends and older traditions, so drawings suit the historical and legendary scenes.

pages.text: What Is a Jack-o’-Lantern? Some of them look spooky. Some of them look funny. Some of them look like detailed works of art. Who knew that so much could be done with pumpkins? Carved pumpkins are called jack-o’-lanterns. They are a festive sight in windows and on doorsteps and porches. Jack-o’-lanterns are popular decorations around Halloween. When a light is placed inside the hollow center, a jack-o’-lantern glows in the autumn night.
pages.brief: Several carved pumpkins called jack-o’-lanterns glow in the autumn night. They sit in windows, on doorsteps, and on porches. Some have spooky faces, some funny faces, and some detailed artistic designs. A light inside each hollow pumpkin makes the carved faces shine.

pages.text: Children and adults alike enjoy turning pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns. Simple jack-o’- lanterns may have triangle eyes and a toothy grin. Others have scary faces. Some artists carve detailed and festive designs. People started carving pumpkins more than a hundred years ago. Legends say the jack-o’-lantern tradition began even earlier, though, in Ireland. People in Ireland carved their jack-o’-lanterns out of turnips or potatoes.
pages.brief: Children and adults turn pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns. One pumpkin has triangle eyes and a toothy grin, another a scary face, and an artist carves a detailed festive design. Nearby, people in Ireland carve jack-o’-lanterns from turnips and potatoes, as legends say the tradition began there.

pages.text: Why did the Irish start this tradition? And where did the name jack-o’-lantern come from, anyway? Many stories are told about its origins. A common one from the nineteenth century tells of a man named Stingy Jack. The legend says that Stingy Jack was cheap. That’s how he earned his nickname. He also liked to play tricks on everyone. Stingy Jack was so mischievous that when he died, he was cursed to roam the land forever. He had to live alone in the darkness. He carved a turnip and put a light inside to guide him. The Irish called his ghost “Jack of the Lantern” and then simply “Jack-o’-lantern.”
pages.brief: In a nineteenth-century legend, Stingy Jack is a mischievous man who plays tricks and is called cheap. After he dies, he is cursed to roam the land forever alone in darkness. He carries a carved turnip with a light inside to guide him, and the Irish call his ghost Jack of the Lantern.

pages.text: Modern Jack-o’-Lanterns Eventually, the Stingy Jack tradition became part of a night called All Hallows’ Eve. People throughout Europe lit bonfires. They also wore costumes to keep roaming ghosts away. In Ireland, people hollowed out turnips and potatoes and carved scary faces on them. They placed a light inside to keep mischievous spirits like Stingy Jack away from their homes. These were the first jack-o’-lanterns. Soon, people in Scotland and England started to follow the practice of carving vegetables on this night. The English used beets to make jack-o’-lanterns. All Hallows’ Eve later became known as Halloween.
pages.brief: On All Hallows’ Eve in Europe, people light bonfires and wear costumes to keep roaming ghosts away. In Ireland, people hollow out turnips and potatoes, carve scary faces, and place a light inside to keep mischievous spirits like Stingy Jack from their homes. People in Scotland and England follow the practice, and the English use beets.

pages.text: When Irish, English, and Scottish people immigrated to the United States, they brought the jack-o’-lantern tradition with them. They soon found that pumpkins, which grew in the United States, worked well as jack-o’-lanterns. By the 1920s, pumpkin carving became common across America. Today, carving jack-o’-lanterns is an important part of Halloween, just like trick-or-treating and wearing costumes. Every autumn, people visit pumpkin patches, farms, and vegetable stands to pick just the right pumpkin. About 1.5 billion pounds (more than 680 million kg) of pumpkins are grown in the United States each year.
pages.brief: Irish, English, and Scottish immigrants bring the jack-o’-lantern tradition to the United States. They find that pumpkins grown there work well for carving. By the 1920s pumpkin carving is common across America. Today, every autumn, people visit pumpkin patches, farms, and vegetable stands to pick just the right pumpkin.

pages.text: Carving Jack-o’-Lanterns Pumpkins that are firm, smooth, and free of marks work well for jack-o’-lanterns. A pumpkin that will stay upright is the safer choice. If it tilts to one side, the light inside may not stay in place. Some people buy carving kits with tools and art patterns to make a great jack-o’-lantern. Other pumpkin carvers use their own tools and designs. Some even carve freehand.
pages.brief: A person chooses a firm, smooth pumpkin without marks. The pumpkin stands upright so the light inside will stay in place. Nearby are carving kits with tools and art patterns. Other pumpkin carvers use their own tools and designs, and some carve freehand.

pages.text: The first step in carving a pumpkin is to cut a hole in the top. This forms the lid. Always have a parent help out while carving with a knife. Next, the inside flesh and the seeds can be scooped out until the pumpkin is clean and hollow. Many people roast the pumpkin seeds for a healthy snack. People also use the pumpkin flesh to make tasty pies, breads, and soups. No part of the pumpkin need go to waste.
pages.brief: A child and a parent cut a hole in the top of a pumpkin to make a lid. The parent helps with the knife. They scoop out the inside flesh and seeds until the pumpkin is clean and hollow. The seeds can be roasted for a snack, and the flesh can make pies, breads, and soups.

pages.text: The next step is to draw a design on the pumpkin. When the design is finished, it’s time to carve. People can carve faces, animals, designs, or a message. They can also use stencils or even paint. Every jack-o’- lantern is a special work of art. After the pumpkin is carved, a candle or other light can be placed inside. Then the pumpkin lid can go back on top. It’s best to display a jack-o’-lantern within a few days of carving. After a few days, the pumpkin may spoil and lose shape.
pages.brief: A person draws a design on a pumpkin, then carves it into a face, an animal, a design, or a message. They may use stencils or paint. After carving, a candle or other light is placed inside and the lid goes back on top. The finished jack-o’-lantern is displayed within a few days before the pumpkin may spoil.

pages.text: Jack-o’-Lantern Events Many cities host jack-o’-lantern festivals to display their artistic pumpkins. Some of the pumpkins feature traditional scary faces. Creative carvers have also fashioned cartoon characters, animals, and other detailed designs. In Hudson Valley, New York, thousands of jack-o’-lanterns make up a special display. This festive event features sound effects and music. Hundreds of pumpkins lie side by side to form snakes and dinosaurs. The event even has a pumpkin planetarium!
pages.brief: Many cities host jack-o’-lantern festivals with artistic pumpkins. Some feature traditional scary faces, while creative carvers fashion cartoon characters, animals, and detailed designs. In Hudson Valley, New York, thousands of jack-o’-lanterns make up a festive display with sound effects and music. Hundreds of pumpkins lie side by side to form snakes, dinosaurs, and even a pumpkin planetarium.

pages.text: A huge display in Los Angeles, California, features pumpkin cars, dinosaurs, and carvings of sports, television, and movie stars. People can watch as the artists carve their pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns. Giant Jack-o’-Lantern An artist carves one of the largest jack-o’-lanterns ever recorded. It weighed more than 1,800 pounds (816 kg)! The record-breaking pumpkin was as heavy as a cow. The artist beat his own Guinness World Record for largest jack-o’-lantern. He had earned that record five years earlier.
pages.brief: In Los Angeles, California, a huge display features pumpkin cars, dinosaurs, and carvings of sports, television, and movie stars. People watch artists carve pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns. An artist also carves one of the largest jack-o’-lanterns ever recorded, weighing more than 1,800 pounds, as heavy as a cow, beating his own Guinness World Record.

pages.text: Recently, the town of Keene, New Hampshire, broke a world record for the most lit jack-o’- lanterns on display. The town boasted a whopping thirty thousand lit jack-o’-lanterns! Halloween Under the Sea Carved pumpkins are even displayed underwater. Some aquarium workers put carved pumpkins in large ocean tanks each autumn. No one knows what the fish think, but visitors enjoy the festive sight.
pages.brief: In Keene, New Hampshire, the town breaks a world record with thirty thousand lit jack-o’-lanterns on display. Elsewhere, aquarium workers put carved pumpkins in large ocean tanks each autumn. Fish swim around them, though no one knows what the fish think. Visitors enjoy the festive underwater sight.

pages.text: The Tradition Continues Carving pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns is a fun activity for people of all ages. Pumpkins can be carved with a scary face or detailed artwork, or be used as part of a larger display. However people carve them, jack-o’-lanterns are a sure sign that Halloween is around the corner. Jack-o’-lantern designs are only limited by the carver’s imagination. What kind of jack-o’-lantern would you make?
pages.brief: People of all ages carve pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns. Some carve a scary face, some create detailed artwork, and others use pumpkins as part of a larger display. However people carve them, jack-o’-lanterns are a sure sign that Halloween is around the corner. The designs are limited only by the carver’s imagination.

books.title: What Happens When You Flush?
books.art_why: Cutaway sewers, treatment steps, and 1800s streets are clearer as drawings than as photos.

pages.text: What Happens What Happens When You Flush When You Flush What Happens What Happens When Yo When Yo Written by Lisa Meltzer.
pages.brief: A circular swirl of blue water fills the scene, spinning with quiet energy down into a dark drain. Soft lines suggest movement and a hidden path below, inviting curiosity about where flushed water goes after it disappears.

pages.text: What Happens What Happens When You Flush? When You Flush?
pages.brief: A close-up view of water rushing around a bend inside a pipe, carrying tiny bits of waste out of sight. The pipe disappears into steady darkness, showing that the flush begins a long, hidden journey.

pages.text: Introduction SWOOSH! You hear this sound every time you flush a toilet. Did you ever stop to wonder where everything that you flush down winds up? Getting rid of waste is often a complex process. That process can stretch over (or under) many miles in your city or town. First, the Flush.
pages.brief: A toilet flushes with a swirling swoosh, sending water and waste down into a dark pipe. Below the floor, the long pipe stretches far underground and away through a town, showing that the journey has only just begun.

pages.text: What Makes Up My Sewage? Where Does Waste Come From? Where Does It Go? Human waste is called sewage. In most homes, it is created by using the toilet, sink, or anything that makes water dirty. If all this sewage reached our drinking water, it would make it unsafe. For more than two billion people worldwide, waste either piles up on the land or runs into lakes and rivers. Millions of people die each year, sick from drinking water that sewage has made unsafe. Sewage treatment experts are working hard to solve this problem, but it is a huge task.
pages.brief: Sewage flows from a home toilet and sink, making water dirty. A wide landscape shows waste piling on land and running into lakes and rivers, while treatment experts look concerned about the huge problem of unsafe drinking water.

pages.text: Lucky for us, the sewer pipes in our homes don’t just empty into our drinking water. Instead, in many cities and towns, all of this dirty water ends up in the local sewer. Two Underground Systems.
pages.brief: Under a row of homes, small pipes carry dirty water away from sinks and toilets. These pipes join a larger local sewer instead of emptying into clear drinking water. A second set of underground pipes runs alongside the first.

pages.text: Inside the Treatment Plant Small sewer pipes join up to form bigger and bigger pipes. The sewage moves through these pipes to a sewage treatment plant. The water is cleaned there. Things in the water that can make people sick are removed.
pages.brief: Small sewer pipes join into larger and larger pipes underground, carrying a steady flow of sewage toward a treatment plant building. Inside the plant, machines clean the water and remove harmful things that could make people sick.

pages.text: Not all sewage treatment systems are alike. One common type cleans sewage in the following way: STEP 1 A big screen (think of a giant kitchen strainer) removes large items such as rocks, sticks, and garbage. That way, they don’t jam up the treatment plant’s machines. STEP 2 What is left over after this process is called sludge. It is thick, dirty water. The treatment plant helps bacteria grow in the sludge. These bacteria eat the sludge to break it down.
pages.brief: At a treatment plant, a giant screen like a kitchen strainer catches rocks, sticks, and garbage before machines can jam. Beyond it, thick dirty sludge sits in a tank while bacteria grow and begin breaking the sludge down.

pages.text: STEP 3 Next, the broken-down sludge is sent to another machine. Here, all of the solid waste settles to the bottom. The water at the top is sent to a filter that cleans it. Once it’s safe, this water can be sent to a stream, lake, or the sea.
pages.brief: Broken-down sludge flows into another machine. Solid waste settles at the bottom while clearer water at the top moves to a filter. After cleaning, the safe water flows out toward a stream, lake, or the sea.

pages.text: STEP 4 The solids are sent to a giant tank called a digester. There, a second kind of bacteria eats much of the sludge. The digester breaks down the solid sludge again and pulls more water from it. About half of the sludge turns into gas. Some of the gas helps power the plant’s machines. The other half of the sludge is dried. It’s often used on farm fields to help grow crops.
pages.brief: Solid sludge enters a huge digester tank where a second kind of bacteria breaks it down and pulls out more water. About half turns into gas that helps power the plant; the dried half is spread on farm fields for crops.

pages.text: The Septic Tank The Septic System— Another Way to Deal with Waste Many homes in the country are far from each other. Building a system large enough to serve homes so far away from one another wouldn’t make much sense. Instead, each home sends human waste into a septic tank. This is a small sewage treatment system for only one home.
pages.brief: In the countryside, homes sit far apart, so one large sewer system would not make sense. Each home sends its human waste into a small septic tank buried nearby, a treatment system just for that single house.

pages.text: The septic tank is buried in the yard near the home. Any waste from the home runs into the tank. Inside the tank, the solids drop to the bottom. The liquid runs out through underground pipes into the yard and spreads into the soil. The liquid is filtered as it moves through the soil. This pulls out harmful things before they reach drinking water. The septic tank collects all of the solid sludge, which builds up over time. When there is too much sludge in the tank, a septic business must pump it out.
pages.brief: A septic tank is buried in a yard near a country home. Waste flows in and solids drop to the bottom, while liquid drains through underground pipes into the soil. The soil filters the liquid, and a septic truck pumps out sludge when too much builds up.

pages.text: Sewage Through the Ages Think these systems are yucky? Think again. The first sewerage systems were built thousands of years ago in places such as the Middle East. These early systems sent human waste with harmful bacteria away from cities—and directly into nearby water. The water made people sick.
pages.brief: Thousands of years ago in the Middle East, early sewer systems carried human waste away from cities. The waste, full of harmful bacteria, flowed directly into nearby water. People who used that water became sick.

pages.text: Even by the 1800s, large cities like New York still had a hard time with their waste. People’s homes had no toilets. Sometimes they just had a hole in the ground. Since there was no way to flush, human waste would pile up in the hole. Some people allowed their waste to spill over and wash into the streets. It would pile up where people walked and children played. The smell was awful.
pages.brief: In the 1800s, many homes in large cities like New York had no toilets, only a hole in the ground. Waste piled up, sometimes spilled into the streets, and collected where people walked and children played. The smell was awful.

pages.text: Experts began to understand that streets flowing with waste were making people sick. New York City began building sewerage systems so the waste would have somewhere to go. By 1914, it had nearly 850 miles (1,368 km) of sewer lines. Today in the United States, waste disappears down toilets and sinks as if by magic. Now you know how it really works, though. So the next time you flush, take a moment to thank your modern sewerage system!
pages.brief: Experts realized waste flowing through streets made people sick, so New York City built sewer lines, nearly 850 miles by 1914. Today waste disappears down toilets and sinks as if by magic, but now the hidden journey through modern sewers is clear.

books.title: Route 66
books.art_why: The highway, attractions and 20th-century events are real, photographable subjects.

pages.text: Introduction It’s 1957. You take the top down on your red sports car. Rock ’n’ roll music blasts from the speakers. Ahead of you is nothing but open road. Could this drive get any better? Then you pass an ice cream cone that’s three stories tall. Your mouth waters. Should you stop? Wait—there’s a cheeseburger the size of a bus. Time for a quick lunch instead! When it’s time to rest for the night, you park next to a hotel room shaped like a teepee. What a fun day it was on the road! Who knows what tomorrow will bring? You’ve just taken a road trip down America’s favorite highway, Route 66.
pages.brief: A red sports car with its top down drives along an open road in 1957, rock ’n’ roll music blasting from the speakers. Ahead stands a three-story ice cream cone, then a cheeseburger the size of a bus. At night the car parks beside a hotel room shaped like a teepee.

pages.text: America’s Main Street Have you ever seen a road map of the United States? It looks a lot like a spiderweb. Huge highways zigzag from coast to coast. They connect nearly every city in between. Getting around is easy. Just jump in a car and hit the road! A hundred years ago, driving across the country wasn’t quite so easy. Most “roads” were just small dirt trails. Cars often broke down, got stuck in mud, or popped tires on jagged rocks. In the 1920s, the United States government created new highways to make driving easier. One highway stretched 2,400 miles (3,862 km) from Chicago, Illinois, to Los Angeles, California. Its name was Route 66. Some people fondly called it the "Main Street of America.”
pages.brief: A road-map view of the United States shows huge highways zigzagging like a spiderweb from coast to coast and connecting cities. Below, early dirt trails are muddy, with a broken-down car stuck in mud and another with a popped tire on jagged rocks. In the 1920s, new highways stretch from Chicago to Los Angeles as Route 66.

pages.text: In 1929, hard times hit the United States. Many banks failed. People lost their money, jobs, and homes. The period that followed was known as the Great Depression. Then a series of long periods without rain destroyed many farms. This time period was known as the Dust Bowl era. Suddenly, many people were forced to leave their homes. Many believed they could find jobs in California. Thousands packed up their belongings and made the long journey west. How did they get there? On a new road named Route 66. The Dust Bowl in Literature The Grapes of Wrath, by John Steinbeck, is a classic novel published in 1939. It is about a family fleeing Oklahoma during the Dust Bowl era. They make the long journey down Route 66 to seek work in California.
pages.brief: During the Great Depression and Dust Bowl, banks fail and dry farm fields stretch under a dusty sky. Families pack their belongings onto cars and join thousands traveling west on Route 66, hoping for work in California. One family from Oklahoma makes the long journey, like the family in a classic novel.

pages.text: On December 8, 1941, the United States entered World War II. Soldiers from all over the country had to move to military bases in the West. How did they get there? On Route 66, of course! Restaurants, gas stations, and hotels opened up along the route to serve them. When the war ended in 1945, Americans celebrated. Many bought new cars. They drove west to see sights like the Grand Canyon by way of Route 66!
pages.brief: Soldiers in uniform travel west along Route 66 to military bases, passing restaurants, gas stations, and hotels that serve them during World War II. After the war ends in 1945, families in shiny new cars drive west along Route 66 to see the Grand Canyon.

pages.text: Route 66 in Popular Culture The years after World War II were great days for Route 66. Shiny new cars and yellow cabs traveled up and down the route. In 1946, a song called “Route 66” became a top hit. The song told listeners to “get your kicks on Route Sixty-Six.” This song helped make the highway famous. Then, in 1960, a TV show called Route 66 followed two friends who drove across the country. They were looking for adventures on the road. By 1970, most of the original Route 66 was bypassed by a new highway. However, Route 66 remained part of American popular culture.
pages.brief: Shiny new cars and yellow cabs travel up and down Route 66 after World War II. A radio plays a hit song about Route 66, and a television shows two friends driving across the country. By 1970, a new highway bypasses most of the original route, but Route 66 remains in popular culture.

pages.text: In the year 2000, John Lasseter, the head of Pixar Animation Studios, drove down Route 66 with his family. He fell in love with the colorful art and buildings. He decided to turn his experiences into a Disney-Pixar movie called Cars, which was released in 2006. Lasseter sent a team down Route 66 to do research for the movie. Some of the roadside art they found ended up as characters in Cars. They used Route 66 sights in the movie. For example, the Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, became the Cozy Cone Motel. Many families who saw Cars took their own vacations along Route 66. This helped the route become popular again.
pages.brief: John Lasseter and his family drive along Route 66, looking at colorful roadside art and buildings. A Pixar research team visits the Wigwam Motel, whose teepee rooms inspire a movie motel. Later, families take their own Route 66 vacations after seeing the movie Cars.

pages.text: Route 66 Attractions PACIFIC OCEAN CANADA UNITED STATES CA ATLANTIC OCEAN MO OK NM TX MEXICO 1 Gemini Giant, Wilmington, IL 2 Paul Bunyon, Atlanta, IL 3 Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower, Collinsville, IL 4 Red Rocker, Fanning, MO 5 Blue Whale, Catoosa, OK 6 Slug Bug Ranch, Conway, TX 7 Cadillac Ranch, Amarillo, TX 8 Wigwam Motel, Holbrook, AZ 9 Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch, Oro Grande, CA @ Cabazon Dinosaurs, Cabazon, CA A Chicken Boy, Los Angeles, CA Roadside Attractions Museums, motels, and shops are found all along Route 66. Route 66 is also full of unique art, historic gas stations, and theaters. In addition, travelers can see live shows such as a Native American dance or a rodeo. One thing’s for sure—you won’t be bored on Route 66!
pages.brief: A Route 66 roadside scene is crowded with attractions: the Gemini Giant, a Paul Bunyon statue, a catsup-bottle water tower, a red rocker, a blue whale, bottle trees, half-buried Cadillacs, concrete dinosaurs, and Chicken Boy. Nearby are museums, motels, shops, historic gas stations, theaters, and a Native American dance or rodeo.

pages.text: Cadillac Ranch In 1974, some artists buried ten cars nose down in a field. Visitors have covered them with colorful spray paint.
pages.brief: Ten cars are buried nose-down in a flat field at Cadillac Ranch, their rear ends sticking up. Artists stand nearby in 1974, and visitors spray colorful paint across the cars, covering them with bright layers.

pages.text: Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch Folk artist Elmer Long built Bottle Tree Ranch out of recycled bottles, car parts, and other found objects. When wind blows through the open bottles, the air fills with music. Blue Whale What do you give the woman who has everything? Hugh Davis built his wife an 80-foot (24.4 m) blue whale for their anniversary!
pages.brief: Elmer Long’s Bottle Tree Ranch rises in the desert, made of recycled bottles, car parts, and found objects; wind passes through open bottles. Nearby, a giant 80-foot blue whale built by Hugh Davis for his wife’s anniversary sits beside the road.

pages.text: A Land of Giants Route 66 is truly a land of giants. A California factory sold thousands of huge statues to businesses to use for advertising. The factory added costumes to turn the giants into cowboys, astronauts, and even chickens. Many of the biggest statues on Route 66 are food statues. Huge oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones might make your mouth water. Look out the window in Illinois to see the largest catsup bottle in the world!
pages.brief: A California factory displays huge advertising statues dressed as cowboys, astronauts, and chickens. Along Route 66, giant food statues—oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones—tower beside the road. In Illinois, the largest catsup bottle in the world rises outside a car window.
