pages.text: Dinosaurs by the Dozen Route 66 is home to prehistoric creatures of all shapes and sizes. One of these giants might be the largest concrete dinosaur in America. He is 150 feet (45.7 m) long and lives at a dinosaur park in California. Claude Bell built the park to draw visitors to his nearby restaurant, the Wheel Inn.
pages.brief: A California dinosaur park features prehistoric creatures of many shapes and sizes. One huge concrete dinosaur stretches 150 feet long; Claude Bell built the park beside his restaurant, the Wheel Inn, to draw visitors to the roadside attraction.

pages.text: Saving Route 66 As more people visited Route 66, heavy traffic caused damage to the highway. From 1956 through the 1980s, new high-speed highways with many lanes were built around Route 66. As more travelers used these highways, businesses on Route 66 lost customers, and many closed. Peeling paint and boarded-up windows became common sights. In 1999, the United States Congress passed a law to protect Route 66. It gave money to help businesses and towns keep important places open. Now Route 66 is growing popular again. The best way to catch the spirit of Route 66 is to drive it. You’re sure to have an unforgettable American experience of your own!
pages.brief: Heavy traffic damages the old highway, and new multi-lane high-speed highways are built around Route 66 from 1956 through the 1980s. Once-busy businesses close, with peeling paint and boarded-up windows. In 1999, Congress passes a law and gives money to protect Route 66; travelers return to drive it.

books.title: Sled Dogs to the Rescue
books.art_why: The 1925 Alaska serum run is a historical event best shown in period-style illustration.

pages.text: Sled Dogs to the Rescue Page 3: The press photographs one of the sled dog teams, including Balto in the front, for a reenactment of their arrival in Nome. Connections.
pages.brief: A press photographer aims a camera at a sled dog team gathered for a reenactment of their arrival in Nome. Balto stands at the front of the team, harnessed with the other dogs, while the photographer records the group.

pages.text: A Terrible Disease In January 1925, sled dog teams raced in a blizzard through the wilderness of Alaska. They battled through heavy snow and icy winds to save children’s lives.
pages.brief: Sled dog teams race through an Alaskan blizzard in January 1925. Dogs pull sleds through deep snow and icy wind in the wilderness, with mushers bundled against the cold, battling forward to save children’s lives.

pages.text: It all started when a terrible disease spread through the town of Nome, Alaska. Two Native children died. Then others became very sick. They needed medicine right away. Nome’s only doctor ordered medicine. However, none came before the city’s port shut down for the winter. The medicine that could save the children was in Anchorage, almost 1,000 miles (1,600 km) away.
pages.brief: In the town of Nome, Alaska, two Native children have died and others are very sick from a terrible disease. The town’s doctor orders medicine, but the winter port is shut and the medicine is almost 1,000 miles away in Anchorage.

pages.text: The medicine could be delivered part of the way by train. Even so, it was 674 miles (1,085 km) from the last train stop to Nome. The distance was too great for airplanes of that time to fly safely. Sled dogs were first used by Native people to deliver goods in the snow. It was clear that sled dogs were the best way to deliver the medicine. There was a problem, however. The distance was too far for one sled dog team. A relay was the only hope.
pages.brief: A train carries the medicine part of the way, then stops 674 miles from Nome. Airplanes of that time cannot fly the distance safely. Native people’s sled dogs, used to deliver goods in snow, wait with a musher for a relay.

pages.text: The Great Sled Dog Relay More than 20 top mushers, most of them Native Alaskans, were set to take part in the relay. More than 150 sled dogs would also take part. Mushers would hand off the medicine to the next team at different posts along the way. On January 27, the medicine arrived by train where the first sled dog team waited. The package, wrapped in heavy fur to keep the medicine from freezing, was handed off. Nome Nenana Alaska Anchorage sled dog route railroad GULF OF ALASKA A journey from the last train stop to Nome would normally take twenty-five days by sled. The teams raced against time to deliver the medicine.
pages.brief: At a snowy relay post, more than twenty top mushers, most of them Native Alaskans, and over 150 sled dogs prepare to pass the medicine onward. On January 27, a train arrives with the package wrapped in heavy fur. A musher hands the package to the next waiting team.

pages.text: The race to Nome was on. The dogs battled through rough wilderness and high winds in bitterly cold weather. The medicine was passed from team to team. Many times, the mushers had to stop to warm the medicine by a fire. Some of the dogs did not survive the journey.
pages.brief: Sled dogs battle through rough wilderness and high winds in bitterly cold weather. The medicine passes from team to team. Mushers stop beside a fire to warm the medicine. Some dogs do not survive the hard journey.

pages.text: One of the teams was driven by the famous musher Leonhard Seppala. It covered the most dangerous part of the race. The temperature had fallen to –85 degrees Fahrenheit (–65°C). Seppala’s lead dog was a twelve-year-old Siberian husky named Togo.
pages.brief: Famous musher Leonhard Seppala drives his team along the most dangerous part of the race. The temperature has fallen to –85 degrees Fahrenheit. His lead dog is Togo, a twelve-year-old Siberian husky, pulling ahead through the cold.

pages.text: To save time, Togo and his teammates raced over an area of frozen sea in the darkness. The next day, they struggled up snow-packed mountains. They traveled an amazing 91 miles (146 km)—more than any other team.
pages.brief: Togo and his teammates race across an area of frozen sea in darkness. The next day, they struggle up snow-packed mountains. Their team travels 91 miles, more than any other team in the relay.

pages.text: The Dogs Deliver The sled dog teams continued their difficult journey. Gunnar Kaasen and his lead Siberian husky, Balto, left on the second to last leg. They raced through a terrible blizzard.
pages.brief: Gunnar Kaasen and his lead Siberian husky, Balto, leave on the second-to-last leg of the relay. The sled dog team races through a terrible blizzard as they continue the difficult journey toward Nome.

pages.text: Balto led the team through whiteout conditions. At one point, a powerful gust of wind flipped the sled over. The medicine fell in the snow. With bare hands, Kaasen dug through the snow to find the medicine. The bitter cold harmed his fingers, but the medicine was safe.
pages.brief: Balto leads the team through whiteout conditions. A powerful gust of wind flips the sled over, and the medicine falls into the snow. Kaasen digs with bare hands through the snow to find it, harming his fingers, but the medicine is safe.

pages.text: When Kaasen arrived at the hand-off point, the next team was not ready to leave. Kaasen decided to continue on to Nome himself. Just before dawn on February 2, Balto and his teammates arrived in Nome. The journey took only five and a half days. The medicine saved the sick children and stopped the spread of the disease.
pages.brief: Just before dawn on February 2, Balto and his teammates arrive in Nome. Kaasen has continued on himself when the next team is not ready. The journey took five and a half days. The medicine saves the sick children and stops the disease’s spread.

pages.text: After the Race A year after the race, Seppala took his dogs, including Togo, on a tour across the United States. They drew large crowds. He was one of the first to bring the Siberian husky breed to other parts of the country.
pages.brief: A year after the race, Seppala takes his dogs, including Togo, on a tour across the United States. Large crowds gather to see them. He is one of the first to bring the Siberian husky breed to other parts of the country.

pages.text: That same year, a statue of Balto was built in New York City. Balto and some of his teammates were in a dog show that toured the United States. However, they were not treated well. A businessman from Cleveland, Ohio, was upset. He thought the dogs had earned a better life. He arranged for their story to be published in a newspaper. In just ten days, people gave enough money to bring the dogs to Cleveland. They stayed in the Cleveland Zoo for the rest of their lives. Balto is still famous for his bravery. However, every sled dog on that journey helped save the sick children when little hope was left.
pages.brief: A statue of Balto stands in New York City. Balto and some teammates tour in a dog show but are not treated well. A Cleveland businessman has their story published. People give enough money in ten days to bring the dogs to the Cleveland Zoo. Balto is still famous for bravery, and every sled dog helped save the children.

books.title: I Collect That!
books.art_why: Real-world objects, hobbies, museums, and collectors can all be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Do you own a few stuffed animals, video games, or other items that are similar to one another? Then you have a collection and can call yourself a collector!
pages.brief: A young collector stands in a room beside a shelf of stuffed animals and a stack of video games, holding one similar item. The child looks over the gathered objects, which form a personal collection of things that are alike.

pages.text: A collection is a group of objects that are alike. People collect all sorts of things, such as rocks, stickers, cars, and even dirt from different places!
pages.brief: Several collectors show groups of alike objects: rocks in a tray, stickers spread on a table, small cars lined up, and jars of different dirt. Each person points to a collection, and the varied items show that people collect many kinds of things.

pages.text: Collecting Is Cool Collecting things is a great hobby. People collect things that excite them and keep their interest. Different people have different interests. Some people are interested in action figures, while others prefer leaves. Collections can be big or small. You might have one hundred trading cards or ten comic books.
pages.brief: A collector sits among action figures and leaves, sorting or arranging a small group of favorite things. Nearby, a child holds a stack of trading cards, while another holds comic books. They look interested and happy with their collections, which are different sizes and made of different objects.

pages.text: Collecting can bring people together. Meeting and talking to people who collect the same things can help you learn more about your collection. You can also buy, sell, and trade parts of your collection. Do You Know? Collectors often get together at meetings called conventions to learn more about what they collect. Huge conventions happen all over the world for collectors of all kinds of things— from dollhouses to toy trains.
pages.brief: Collectors meet at a busy convention, talking beside tables of dollhouses and toy trains. Some people buy, sell, and trade items while others examine collections together. The room is full of shared interest, with groups chatting and learning more about the things they collect.

pages.text: Keeping a collection can be hard work. Many collectors keep count of their items and take care of them. Collectors usually sort their objects in some way. They might look at age, size, type, or material.
pages.brief: A collector carefully counts items and writes a record while another sorts objects into groups by age, size, type, or material. The items are arranged in tidy rows, and the collectors handle them gently, showing that keeping a collection can take work and care.

pages.text: Common Collections Stamps, coins, masks, and dolls are some of the most popular things people collect. These items are easy to find, and there are many different kinds. People can collect coins or stamps from one country or from many countries around the world. Math Minute Emma counts 34 bookmarks in her collection. She gets 11 more for her birthday. How many bookmarks are in her collection now?
pages.brief: Stamps, coins, masks, and dolls fill display trays and shelves as examples of popular collections. At a table, Emma counts a pile of bookmarks, with some bookmarks set aside in small stacks. She looks focused as she works out how many are in her collection.

pages.text: Some people collect things from places they have visited. When they travel somewhere new, they buy a souvenir. It might be a magnet, key chain, or snow globe with the name or picture of the place.
pages.brief: A traveler stands in a new place, choosing a souvenir from a display of magnets, key chains, and snow globes. Each souvenir shows the place they visited. The collector holds the item, ready to add it to a collection of things from places they have traveled to.

pages.text: Other people collect things they find in nature, such as sticks or shells. They search for items to collect while hiking in the woods or exploring a beach. Many people use their collections to create new things. Some collectors turn their finds into things they can wear, such as a necklace or bracelet made from collected sea glass. Others make works of art. Bottle caps are used to make anything from maps to magnets. Driftwood can be turned into wind chimes.
pages.brief: Collectors search in nature, picking up sticks in the woods and shells on a beach. Later, they turn finds into wearable pieces and art: sea glass becomes a necklace or bracelet, bottle caps become maps or magnets, and driftwood becomes a wind chime. The natural objects are gathered and reused.

pages.text: You Collect What? Some people collect objects based on a specific theme, such as a type of animal. One woman set the world record for owl collectibles. She owns more than eighteen thousand things related to owls—owl toys, owl T-shirts, and more. Wowser! Barney Smith’s collection of toilet seats became so large that he made a museum to display them. These aren’t regular toilet seats—they’re works of art! Stop by the Toilet Seat Art Museum in Texas to check out his collection of more than one thousand toilet seats.
pages.brief: A woman’s large owl collection fills shelves with owl toys and owl T-shirts. In Texas, Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum displays rows of artistic toilet seats. The collection is huge and unusual, showing how a specific theme can grow into a museum display.

pages.text: It takes time to build a collection. It can be rewarding to find an item you’ve been looking for, such as a particular lunch box. Some people enjoy having to work hard to add to their collection. Other people prefer to collect things that are easy to find or make. A woman even made a museum to house her collection of burnt food.
pages.brief: A collector searches shelves for a particular lunch box, reaching toward the item with care. In another setting, a woman’s museum houses her collection of burnt food. The scenes show that building a collection takes time, effort, and patience, whether the objects are hard to find or easy to make.

pages.text: Start Your Own Collection If you want to start a collection, you don’t have to look far. You can start in your own house with common items, such as bars of soap or hats. Do you have fruit in your fruit bowl? Check out the sticker labels. One woman has over 10,000 fruit sticker labels in her collection, including more than 8,500 banana labels! The next time you eat at a restaurant, grab some sugar packets. One man has a collection of more than 14,000 sugar packets. If you start now, you might have an even bigger collection one day.
pages.brief: In a home, a collector looks at common items such as bars of soap and hats. A fruit bowl holds fruit with small stickers, and stacks of fruit stickers are gathered nearby. At a restaurant table, a man places sugar packets into a collection, with many packets already sorted.

pages.text: Collections can also be really strange. Some people collect air sickness bags and shopping lists other people have left behind in supermarkets. Collecting things is a fun way to spend your time, meet friends, and learn new things. If you don’t already have a collection, maybe it’s time to start one.
pages.brief: Collectors show strange collections: air sickness bags and shopping lists left behind in supermarkets. Nearby, a cheerful group of collectors talks together, surrounded by their unusual finds. The scene suggests that collecting can be fun, can bring friends together, and can help people learn new things.

books.title: Acadia National Park
books.art_why: Acadia National Park is a real place today, so a photograph is possible.

pages.text: National P ark ACADIA.
pages.brief: A sweeping view of Acadia National Park, presenting the park as a whole. The scene introduces the place named in the book, with open space and daylight around it, without focusing on one single visitor, animal, or building.

pages.text: First to See the Sun Acadia National Park is one of the first places in the United States to see the Sun rise. Look on a map and you’ll understand why. Maine stretches farther east than any of the other forty-nine states. Acadia has tall peaks that catch the first rays of sunlight.
pages.brief: The Sun rises over Acadia National Park, lighting the tall peaks first. A map view shows Maine stretching farther east than the other forty-nine states, explaining why Acadia is one of the first places in the United States to see the sunrise.

pages.text: Land That Meets the Sea More than two million people visit Acadia National Park each year. The park packs a lot into a small space: beautiful coastline, islands, forests, lakes, and rocks.
pages.brief: More than two million visitors explore Acadia National Park, a small park packed with beautiful coastline, islands, forests, lakes, and rocks. People move through the varied landscape, showing how much the park holds in a small space.

pages.text: Here, mountains rise from the sea. At 1,530 feet (466 m), Cadillac Mountain is the tallest. Because of its amazing view, it’s also the most crowded. Acadia has more than 40 miles (64 km) of coastline. During low tides, the ocean leaves behind pools of water. Inside these pools live sea stars, sea cucumbers, hot pink seaweed, and more.
pages.brief: Cadillac Mountain rises from the sea at 1,530 feet, drawing a crowd to its amazing view. Along more than 40 miles of coastline, low tide leaves pools of water where sea stars, sea cucumbers, and hot pink seaweed live.

pages.text: Tide pools come and go—just like tides. Try to visit the tide pools when the tide is going out. You’ll have more time to explore them.
pages.brief: Tide pools appear and disappear with the tides along Acadia’s shore. A visitor explores a tide pool as the tide goes out, when the water is still shallow and there is more time to look at the pool’s creatures.

pages.text: Wildlife Acadia is one of the best bird-watching spots in the country— 338 kinds of birds have been seen there. Each autumn, thousands of raptors fly over Acadia as they migrate from Canada for the winter.
pages.brief: Bird-watchers watch Acadia’s skies, where 338 kinds of birds have been seen. In autumn, thousands of raptors fly over the park as they migrate from Canada for the winter, filling the air above the landscape.

pages.text: Return of the Falcon Peregrine falcons are one of the fastest animals on Earth. Long ago, they nested on Acadia’s mountains. Their speed didn’t save them from humans, though, whose actions killed many of them. By the 1960s, peregrine falcons were gone from the park. For years, Acadia worked to bring the falcons back. In 1991, the park saw its first falcon chicks in thirty-five years. Since then, chicks have been born in the park every year.
pages.brief: Peregrine falcons fly fast over Acadia’s mountains, where they once nested long ago. After humans killed many and the falcons disappeared by the 1960s, the park worked for years to bring them back. In 1991, the first chicks in thirty-five years appear, and chicks have been born every year since.

pages.text: Compared to many national parks, Acadia is not very big. It doesn’t have many big mammals, either. It has lots of small mammals, though, such as foxes and porcupines.
pages.brief: Compared with many national parks, Acadia is small and lacks many big mammals. Instead, small mammals live around the park, including foxes and porcupines moving through the landscape. The scene focuses on these smaller animals in their natural surroundings.

pages.text: A Park Made Piece by Piece The most amazing fact about Acadia may be that it became a national park at all. Native people called the Wabanaki lived on the land for 12,000 years. Wabanaki means “People of the Dawnland.” The Wabanaki built canoes, fished, hunted, and gathered plants around the area. The Wabanaki Today The Wabanaki are made up of five tribes. They live in Northern Maine and parts of Canada. Those who live near Acadia build canoes and baskets like their ancestors did. They also guide hunting tourists, sell smoked shellfish, or teach people at the yearly Native American Festival and Basket Makers Market.
pages.brief: Wabanaki people, the People of the Dawnland, have lived on the land for 12,000 years, building canoes, fishing, hunting, and gathering plants. Today five tribes live in Northern Maine and parts of Canada; near Acadia they build canoes and baskets, guide hunting tourists, sell smoked shellfish, and teach at the yearly Native American Festival and Basket Makers Market.

pages.text: In the 1600s, French settlers took land from the Wabanaki. British settlers moved north in the 1700s and fought with the French. The fighting and diseases brought by the Europeans killed many Wabanaki. They forced others to leave. The land became the state of Maine in 1820. Rich people came to the rocky coastline to buy land and build fancy summer homes.
pages.brief: In the 1600s, French settlers take land from the Wabanaki. British settlers move north in the 1700s and fight the French. The fighting and European diseases kill many Wabanaki and force others to leave. The land becomes the state of Maine in 1820, and rich people build fancy summer homes on the rocky coastline.

pages.text: The Wabanaki had protected the land for many years. Now, the rich people who owned it wanted to protect it too. A man named George Dorr and others began to donate land to the government. In 1919, that land became The Story of Dorr George Dorr lived alone in a grand house on Mount Desert Island. In order to protect the area, he slowly bought bits of land, then turned around and donated them. By the time he died in 1944, he had spent all his money, but Dorr had made his dream come true. Acadia had become a national park. In fact, it was still growing like a patchwork quilt, piece by piece. Even today, landowners continue to donate land around Acadia.
pages.brief: After the Wabanaki protected the land for years, rich owners want to protect it too. George Dorr lives alone in a grand house on Mount Desert Island; he buys bits of land and donates them. In 1919, the land becomes a national park and by his death in 1944, Dorr has spent all his money making his dream come true.

pages.text: Conclusion Acadia National Park is a place where sea and mountain meet. People come to see them meet and, of course, to watch the Sun rise. After greeting the new day, there is plenty more to see and do in Acadia. Visitors can hike, climb, fish, or ride a bicycle.
pages.brief: Sea and mountain meet in Acadia National Park. People come to see them meet and to watch the Sun rise. After greeting the new day, visitors hike, climb, fish, or ride bicycles, with plenty more to see and do around the park.

pages.text: If you ever get the chance to visit, do!
pages.brief: A visitor takes the chance to visit Acadia National Park, showing the park as a place worth seeing. The scene encourages others to come when they can and to enjoy the park for themselves.

books.title: Rocky Mountain National Park
books.art_why: Rocky Mountain National Park exists today, with real landscapes, animals, roads, and visitors that can be photographed.

pages.text: Rocky Mountain National Park.
pages.brief: A wide view of a national park in the Rocky Mountains shows rugged peaks, dark pine forests, and a bright mountain lake. The land looks wild and open. No roads or buildings interrupt the natural scene.

pages.text: The Best of the Rockies Rocky Mountain National Park (RMNP), in Colorado, shows off the best of the Rocky Mountains. The park includes 415 square miles (668 sq km) of natural beauty. The air is fresh and clean. Its mountain lakes mirror high peaks above them. The park is home to mountain lions, moose, marmots, and many other wild animals. Nature lovers can enjoy the park, whether by car or on foot.
pages.brief: High mountain peaks rise above a still lake that mirrors them. Pine forests cover the slopes, and a moose stands in shallow water while a marmot watches from a rock nearby. A car and walkers show nature lovers enjoying the park.

pages.text: Young Mountains Rocky Mountain National Park is a small part of the Rocky Mountain Range. The Rockies, as they are called, stretch 3,000 miles (4,828 km) from Canada to New Mexico. Compared to other mountain ranges, the Rockies are young. They were pushed up between one hundred million and sixty-five million years ago. Later on, glaciers moved downhill and carved out their valleys.
pages.brief: A long range of rugged Rocky Mountain peaks stretches across the land, with deep valleys between the slopes. The mountains look young and sharp. A wide valley curves downhill, shaped long ago by glaciers moving through the high country.

pages.text: The Rocky Mountains form much of the Continental Divide. This is a rocky spine that runs along North America and divides the way water flows. Water on the western side of the divide flows west toward the Pacific Ocean. Water on the eastern side flows toward the Atlantic Ocean. NORTH AMERICA The Continental Divide United States Mexico.
pages.brief: A high rocky ridge runs like a spine across a broad mountain landscape. Streams on one side flow toward a distant ocean, while streams on the other side flow toward another ocean. The ridge divides the direction the water travels.

pages.text: From Moose to Marmots Rocky Mountain National Park has several different environments. It has wet areas and forests of pine and aspen trees. Mountain wildflowers dot grassy meadows with bright colors in summer. The trees stop growing at about 11,500 feet (3,505 m). This is called the tree line. Above this line, it’s too cold and rocky for trees to grow. Different areas in RMNP are home to different animals. Elk and deer feed along forest edges. Moose wade in watery places and chomp plants there. Bobcats and a few mountain lions and black bears live in the park, too.
pages.brief: A grassy meadow dotted with bright wildflowers meets a forest of pine and aspen trees. Elk and deer feed along the forest edge, a moose wades in a wet place and chomps plants, and a black bear moves near the trees. Above, bare rocky slopes rise past the tree line.

pages.text: Some animals live above the tree line. They include bighorn sheep, Colorado’s state animal. Marmots are one of the largest members of the squirrel family. They can be spotted on warm, sunny rocks, and they squeak loudly if danger is near. In rocky places, pika dash around. They look like big hamsters but are related to rabbits.
pages.brief: On a rocky slope above the tree line, a bighorn sheep stands on a ledge. Nearby, a marmot rests on a warm sunny rock. A small pika dashes between stones in the rocky ground. The animals live in the cold, open high country.

pages.text: About 280 kinds of birds have been seen in RMNP. Eagles and ravens ride on mountain winds. Ptarmigan (TAR-mi-gin) are great at hiding in the open. In summer, their brown and gray feathers blend in with the earth. In winter, their feathers turn white and blend in with the snow.
pages.brief: An eagle and a raven soar on mountain winds above rocky peaks. Below, a ptarmigan in brown and gray summer feathers stands in the open, blending with the earth. Nearby, snow shows how its feathers turn white in winter.

pages.text: Plan a Visit A visit to Rocky Mountain National Park can be carefree or full of adventure. Inside the park, the roads allow drivers to enjoy great views. Trail Ridge Road is the highest paved road in any U.S. national park. As it climbs up and over the Continental Divide, it reaches more than 12,000 feet (3,658 m). This road is closed in winter, when snowdrifts can be more than 20 feet (6 m) deep.
pages.brief: A paved road climbs steeply up and over a high rocky mountain pass. A car carries drivers past wide mountain views. Beside the road, deep snowdrifts show how winter snow can close the route to cars.

pages.text: For people who want to leave behind the sound of traffic, RMNP has hundreds of miles of hiking trails. Some hikers pitch tents near mountain lakes and rushing creeks. Others follow rocky paths to reach mountaintops. At 14,259 feet (4,346 m), Longs Peak is the park’s tallest mountain. Hikers must be very fit to climb it.
pages.brief: Hikers pitch tents beside a mountain lake and a rushing creek. Others follow a rocky path upward toward a tall peak. Longs Peak rises high above them, its summit steep and distant. The hikers look fit and prepared for a long climb.

pages.text: Autumn is a special time to visit the park. Aspen leaves turn bright yellow. People also come to watch and listen to elk. In September and October, bull elk use high-pitched calls to attract females, known as cows.
pages.brief: In autumn, aspen trees glow with bright yellow leaves. People stand quietly to watch and listen as a bull elk lifts his head and gives a high-pitched call. Female elk, called cows, stand nearby in the open.

pages.text: History of Rocky Mountain National Park Ute, Arapaho, and other Native peoples once lived in and traveled through the land that is now Rocky Mountain National Park. Some spent summers camped in the beautiful valleys. Settlers and gold seekers began arriving in this part of the Rockies in the mid-1800s. For settlers headed west, these same mountains were hard to cross.They had to drive their wagons over the steep passes. Others built mining towns, including Estes Park, near what later became one of the park entrances. In 1915, the president signed a law creating Rocky Mountain National Park. This was followed by a building boom of lodges and roads nearby. However, much of RMNP is still surrounded by forests and wilderness areas.
pages.brief: Ute and Arapaho people rest at a summer camp in a beautiful valley. In the distance, settlers drive wagons over a steep mountain pass, and a small mining town sits near the valley. Forests and wilderness surround the scene.

pages.text: A Popular Park Rocky Mountain National Park is one of the most popular national parks in the United States. Each year, more than four million people visit from around the world. During the summer months, the park can get crowded. Sometimes there are traffic jams. Many people now ride buses inside the park rather than drive their cars. Four Million and Counting.
pages.brief: In summer, a park road is crowded with cars in a traffic jam. Buses carry many visitors from around the world. People look out at the mountain scenery. The busy scene shows how popular the national park has become.

pages.text: Still, anyone willing to lace up their hiking boots can go on an adventure in this park. It is a national—and a natural—treasure.
pages.brief: A hiker sits on a rock beside a trail and laces up sturdy hiking boots. Behind, mountain peaks, pine forests, and open slopes stretch into the distance. The trail leads into wild country, inviting anyone ready for an adventure.

books.title: Manatees
books.art_why: Manatees are real animals living today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Early sailors saw manatees and thought they were mermaids. That is hard to imagine. Manatees have a gentle and sweet appearance, but they don’t look like mermaids! Manatees are marine mammals. They belong to a group of mammals called Sirenia. This name comes from the old belief that manatees were sea sirens. They are sometimes called sea cows because they graze on plants for many hours at a time, like cows do. They also eat huge amounts of food like cows do. Description.
pages.brief: Early sailors on an old sailing ship lean over the side, gazing at a manatee swimming in warm shallow water. The manatee has a gentle, rounded look and grazes on underwater plants like a sea cow, feeding for many hours.

pages.text: Manatees have rounded bodies and small heads. They have a paddle-shaped tail that helps them move through the water. Large front flippers help them to steer. They have pudgy, wrinkled faces that look a little like the face of a walrus. They have heavy, solid bones. Scientists think their heavy bones keep them from floating too high in the water. Manatees are not close relatives of whales, dolphins, or walruses, even though all of these are marine mammals. They are also not closely related to cows. The closest well-known living relative of the manatee is the elephant.
pages.brief: A manatee floats in clear water, showing its rounded body, small head, paddle-shaped tail, large front flippers, and pudgy, wrinkled face. Its sturdy build suggests heavy, solid bones. An elephant stands on a nearby shore, hinting at the manatee's closest well-known living relative.

pages.text: There are three kinds of manatees—the Amazonian Distribution of Manatees manatee, the West African manatee, and the West Indian manatee. West Indian manatees are divided into two types: Florida manatees and Antillean manatees. This map shows where manatees live today. West Indian manatees are about 3 meters (10 ft) long and weigh about 545 kg (1,200 lbs). West African manatees are about the same size. Amazonian manatees are smaller. They measure 2.7 meters (9 ft) or less in length. They weigh 455 kg (1,000 lbs) or less.
pages.brief: A world map shows shaded river and coastal regions where Amazonian, West African, and West Indian manatees live today. Three manatees of different sizes swim in fresh water and salt water, with the smaller Amazonian manatee beside the larger West Indian and West African manatees.

pages.text: Habitat and Habits Manatees live in both fresh water and salt water. They like shallow water in bays and rivers and along ocean coasts. They like water temperatures higher than 20 degrees C (68 degrees F). A thick layer of blubber protects them from the cold. But they cannot survive if it gets too cold. Manatees are gentle, harmless creatures that have no way to defend themselves. Staying close to shore keeps them safe from sharks and other predators in the open ocean. Canada Manatees migrate between summer and winter feeding grounds. Scientists have tagged some manatees with radio transmitters to track their movements. They tracked one West Indian manatee that traveled more than 2,414 kilometers (1,500 mi) from Florida to Rhode Island. He broke the record for the longest migration by a West Indian manatee.
pages.brief: A manatee swims in warm, shallow water along a coast, with a thick layer of blubber visible under its skin. A small radio transmitter is attached to it. Far offshore, a shark swims in deeper open water. The manatee stays close to shore for safety.

pages.text: Manatees spend up to eight hours a day Do You Know? A manatee may eat over 45.5 kilograms (100 lbs) of plants each day. eating. They are vegetarians that feed on floating or underwater plants. A manatee can eat up to fifteen percent of its body weight each day. Imagine if you did that. The average person would have to eat almost 11.5 kilograms (25 lbs) of food a day. Manatees spend up to twelve hours a day resting. They may rest on the surface of the water or at the bottom. When resting, they can stay underwater for up to twenty minutes at a time. When they are active, they need to come up for air every three to five minutes. Manatees mostly live alone and often play alone. They may roll over and over in the water. They may swim on their backs, or bodysurf. Even though they don’t live in herds, the search for warm water sometimes brings them together. Manatees often gather in large numbers near power plants that give off heated water. Dozens of manatees may be found together because the warm water feels good to them. Do You Know? A manatee’s body is often covered with a coat of algae. This makes some manatees look like they have green fur!
pages.brief: A manatee eats floating and underwater plants in shallow water. Another manatee rests at the surface, and one rolls over on its back. A green coat of algae covers a manatee's body. In the distance, several manatees gather near warm water from a power plant.

pages.text: While manatees are loners, they do sometimes get together. When they do, they get along well with each other. Sometimes manatees seem to kiss each other when they meet. They also nibble and groom each other. They often touch flippers and roll together as though they are dancing. Manatees talk with each other using chirps, squeaks, squeals, and whistles. pages.text: Threats to Survival All manatees are in great danger of becoming extinct, or dying out completely. Their numbers are low because of many reasons. One reason is that they have been hunted for food and for their hides. Manatees also can die when they get trapped in fishing nets. books.title: Giant Pandas
books.art_why: Giant pandas and their habitats are real animals and places that exist today.

pages.text: Meet the Giant Panda Giant pandas are among the most loved animals in the world. They are easily recognized by their thick black-and-white fur. Giant pandas are a kind of bear. Wild giant pandas remain only in the forest-covered mountains of central China. They are so rare that they have become a symbol of Earth’s endangered animals.
pages.brief: A wild giant panda with thick black-and-white fur quietly stands among trees on a forest-covered mountain in central China. The bear-like animal is shown in its natural mountain habitat, representing a rare and endangered species.

pages.text: Do You Know? Pandas do not hibernate like other bears do. They must eat year-round to get enough nutrients. Food and Feeding The word panda means “bamboo eater.” Bamboo, a kind of very tall grass, is plentiful in the cold, damp mountains where pandas live. It makes up almost all of a panda’s diet. Bamboo is low in the nutrients that pandas need. For this reason, pandas must eat an amazing amount of bamboo to get enough nutrients. An adult panda spends as many as sixteen hours a day eating up to 18 kilograms (40 lbs) of bamboo.
pages.brief: An adult giant panda sits among tall bamboo in a cold, damp mountain forest. It holds bamboo stalks and eats them, showing the enormous amount of bamboo it needs each day. The panda does not hibernate and must feed year-round.

pages.text: Giant Panda Life Cycle Giant pandas are mammals. Like all mammals, they give birth to live young and nurse them. A female panda begins having cubs when she is five or six years old. Then she gives birth to only one or two cubs every few years. A mother panda must work full-time to care for just one baby. She usually raises only one cub and ignores any others, which then die of neglect.
pages.brief: A mother giant panda lies with one tiny newborn cub close to her body. The cub is blind and helpless at birth and depends completely on her mother’s care. The mother panda focuses on the single cub she will raise.

pages.text: At birth, newborn pandas are tiny and blind. They completely depend on their mother’s care. Because they are so helpless, they are vulnerable to predators. A baby panda develops slowly. It cannot walk until the age of four months. It stops nursing and begins eating bamboo by the age of one year. During the first two years of its life, a panda cub stays close to its mother. It learns how to survive in the forest. The cub figures out how to find the best food plants. It learns how to tell friend from enemy when it meets other animals. A young panda’s biggest dangers are leopards and wild dogs.
pages.brief: A young giant panda cub stays close to its mother in the forest. The cub is still learning to find food plants and to tell friend from enemy. In the background, a leopard and wild dogs show the dangers the vulnerable young panda faces.

pages.text: A panda is an adult by the age of three. It settles in an area called a home range, where it feeds alone. Each panda gives other pandas signs to keep away from its home range. One sign is a smelly liquid that the panda releases from its body and rubs on tree trunks. A panda also marks the edges of its home range by scratching the bark of tree trunks. Are Pandas Really Giant? Giant pandas are actually one of the smaller kinds of bears. They are called “giant pandas” to distinguish them from red pandas, which also live in bamboo forests in China. Turn to page 11 to see a red panda. Grizzly bear Giant panda.
pages.brief: An adult giant panda lives alone in its home range and marks the edges by rubbing a smelly liquid on tree trunks and scratching bark. A grizzly bear stands beside a giant panda, showing that giant pandas are one of the smaller kinds of bears.

pages.text: Female pandas usually live alone in their home range. Males roam more widely and are more aware of their neighbors. When it is time to mate, males know where to find females and where to find their male rivals. Males fight for the right to mate with a female by pushing and bumping each other.
pages.brief: Two male giant pandas push and bump each other in a bamboo forest while competing for the right to mate. A female panda is nearby in her home range. The males have roamed widely and are aware of their neighbors.

pages.text: Giant Panda Survival Giant pandas are in great danger of becoming extinct. No one is sure how many are left because they are hard to find and count. But scientists think that only about 1,864 giant pandas are still alive in the wild. The biggest threat to pandas is the destruction of their forest homes. China’s population is growing fast. Bamboo forests are being cleared for wood and farmland. Pandas are also in danger from hunters who want to sell their coats. Pandas are easy targets because they move slowly. The Chinese government now has strict laws to protect pandas. There are more than sixty preserves to protect their habitat.
pages.brief: A giant panda stands in a shrinking bamboo forest in China. Around it, trees have been cleared for wood and farmland, showing the destruction of its forest home. The slow-moving panda is vulnerable to hunters and is protected in a preserve.

pages.text: Many zoos now have panda breeding programs. Scientists are studying how to help pandas survive in the wild. People around the world are working hard to keep giant pandas alive. Do You Know? The red panda is not a close relative of the giant panda, even though it has a similar name. Red pandas are relatives of raccoons. They live in the same bamboo forests as giant pandas.
pages.brief: In a zoo enclosure, a giant panda is cared for as part of a breeding program while scientists watch and study it. In the same bamboo forest habitat, a red panda sits among branches; red pandas are relatives of raccoons, not close relatives of giant pandas.

books.title: Totem Poles
books.art_why: Traditional Native carvings, ceremonies, and historical events from the past suit drawn illustrations.

pages.text: Monuments of Cedar Carving a bird from a block of wood is hard work. Imagine carving animals on a piece of wood as long as a tree trunk! Native peoples living along the Pacific Northwest Coast have been doing that for hundreds of years. These carvings are called totem poles. Pacific Northwest Coast.
pages.brief: Native carvers along the Pacific Northwest Coast work on a long cedar log, carving animal figures into wood as long as a tree trunk. The finished carvings are totem poles, standing among tall trees near the coast.

pages.text: Totem Poles Speak Totem poles are carved in different styles and for different reasons. The figures carved on the poles have special meanings and help record history. Memorial poles describe someone’s life or a special event. Other totem poles tell the history of a clan, or family group. Still others welcome visitors.
pages.brief: Several totem poles with different carvings stand together. One pole has figures that record a memorial, another tells the history of a clan, and a third welcomes visitors. Each pole has its own style and arrangement of carved figures.

pages.text: Some totem poles are part of a house. House poles are carved into the doorways, on the outside corners, or on poles that support the roof. These poles show the wealth and status of the family.
pages.brief: A family house has totem poles built into its doorway, on its outside corners, and as supports for the roof. Carved figures cover the poles, showing the family’s wealth and status. The poles are part of the house itself.

pages.text: Mortuary poles are like gravestones. The carvings on the pole honor the life of a person who has died. They tell about important events and family relationships in the dead person’s life. Some totem poles welcome visitors to a village. These are usually single human figures. They are put near a beach or stream to show visitors that they are welcome.
pages.brief: A mortuary pole stands like a gravestone, its carvings honoring a dead person and telling about important family events and relationships. Nearby, a single carved human figure stands by a beach or stream, welcoming visitors to the village.

pages.text: A Legend of Black Bear This totem pole stands in a park in Canada. It tells how Killer Whale clan* took Black Bear for its crest, or special symbol. One day, a hunter went into the mountains looking for mountain goats. Black Bear captured him and brought the hunter to his den. The man lived with Black Bear. Although they became friends, the man missed his village. After two years, Black Bear let the man go home. By now, the man looked like a bear. The villagers ran from him. Finally, one kind man rubbed medicine on the man’s body. Soon the man looked human again. He took Black Bear as his crest. His friend Black Bear always protected the man’s family. Hunter Kind Man Black Bear Black Bear’s human form.
pages.brief: In a Canadian park, a totem pole shows Black Bear and a hunter. In the story, Black Bear captures the hunter in the mountains, keeps him in his den, and later lets him return home; a kind man uses medicine to make the hunter look human again.

pages.text: These illustrations show some common figures on totem poles. While each culture has different stories about them, some traits of each animal remain the same. Raven Bird with a straight beak Raven is a trickster. He can change shape into almost anything, such as a bird, a human, or even a speck of dirt. Bear Round ears, many teeth Bear is a caring, godlike creature that can change to human form. Beaver Long front teeth, flat tail with crisscross lines Beaver is a clever carver. His powerful tail-slap can cause earthquakes or turn him invisible.
pages.brief: Carved figures of Raven, Bear, and Beaver appear on totem poles. Raven has a straight beak and can change shape; Bear has round ears and many teeth and can become human; Beaver has long front teeth and a flat, crisscrossed tail.

pages.text: Watchmen Crouching men with very tall hats Watchmen are human figures who can spot danger from far away. Thunderbird Curly feathers that look like horns Thunderbird is one of the most powerful spirits for many Native peoples. It causes thunder and lightning. It is large enough to catch a whale in its talons. Wolf Pointed ears, long snout, many sharp teeth Wolf is not friendly to humans. He knows the secrets of healing.
pages.brief: A carved Watchman crouches with a very tall hat, a Thunderbird has curly feathers that look like horns, and a Wolf has pointed ears, a long snout, and many sharp teeth. Each figure is shown on a totem pole.

pages.text: Carving a Totem Pole In the past, a clan would hire a master carver to make a totem pole. Today, many museums, businesses, and people around the world also want totem poles created for them. First, they hire a carver and work with them to plan the pole. The carver finds a tree with no knots or bends. The carver cuts down the tree, cuts off the branches, and hauls it to the workshop. Then the carver chips away the soft outer wood.
pages.brief: A carver and a clan plan a totem pole, then choose a straight tree with no knots or bends. The carver cuts down the tree, removes its branches, hauls the trunk to a workshop, and chips away the soft outer wood.

pages.text: Often, a team of carvers works on the totem pole. The master carver draws the designs on the log with charcoal. The master carver works on the bottom figure of the pole. That’s because this figure is the biggest and most important. Everyone can see it up close. Helpers carve and paint other figures on the totem pole. Carving a big pole can take as long as nine months.
pages.brief: A team of carvers works on a large log. The master carver draws designs with charcoal and carves the biggest, most important figure at the bottom, while helpers carve and paint the other figures. The work can take nine months.

pages.text: A Master at Work Today, some Native people of the Northwest Coast still work with wood to make traditional art. You can see totem poles being carved at Saxman Native Village near Ketchikan, Alaska. The village was settled by the Tlingit in 1894. Visitors from all over the world go there each year. They look at the village’s many beautiful totem poles and watch carvers at work. Many of the poles were carved by Nathan Jackson. He won many awards and helped bring Northwest Coast art back to life. He has inspired many other artists.
pages.brief: At Saxman Native Village near Ketchikan, Alaska, visitors look at many totem poles and watch carvers at work. The village was settled by the Tlingit in 1894, and carver Nathan Jackson has won awards and inspired other artists.

pages.text: When the pole is ready, it is brought to the place where it will stand. A potlatch, or special ceremony, is held to celebrate the raising of the pole. People eat, dance, sing, and give gifts. They tell about the events shown on the pole. Prayers and blessings may be said for the pole and for the people who own it. Return of the Potlatch In 1884, the government of British Columbia passed a law that made potlatches illegal. Most Native peoples stopped carving totem poles. But in 1951, the law was dropped and they began carving totem poles again.
pages.brief: People gather for a potlatch ceremony as a finished totem pole is raised. They eat, dance, sing, give gifts, and say prayers and blessings for the pole and its owners. After a long ban, Native peoples begin carving totem poles again in 1951.

pages.text: Totem Poles Come Home European explorers came to the Northwest Coast in the 1800s. They were impressed by the totem poles they found. Many of the poles ended up in museums. In 1990, the United States passed a new law. It said Native peoples would be able to get back property that had been stolen from them. Because of this law, many totem poles are returning to their homes and to the people who created them.
pages.brief: European explorers in the 1800s look at totem poles on the Northwest Coast. Many poles are later shown in museums. In 1990 a new United States law lets Native peoples recover stolen property, and totem poles return to their homes and creators.

books.title: C Is for Canada
books.art_why: The book mixes modern Canada with historical events, ancient scenes, and a glossary, so drawings can cover the whole span.

pages.text: Subject: Greetings from Canada Hey Stephanie, It was so exciting to get your email yesterday! I’ve been looking forward to having a pen pal for some time now. I’m so glad your teacher in Omaha (that’s in Nebraska, right?) contacted mine here in Vancouver (that’s in British Columbia). Do you know where that is?
pages.brief: Jacqueline, a Canadian girl in Vancouver, British Columbia, sits at a computer and writes an excited email to Stephanie in Omaha, Nebraska. She smiles as she welcomes her new pen pal and thinks about whether Stephanie knows where British Columbia is.

pages.text: British Columbia is one of the 10 provinces in Canada (there are three territories, too). We don’t have states like the United States. Anyway, in your last email, you said that you are doing a report on Canada. Is this the kind of information that you’re looking for? If not, could you be more specific? I hope I can help. Your Canadian pen pal, Jacqueline.
pages.brief: Jacqueline continues writing from Vancouver, explaining that British Columbia is one of ten provinces in Canada, which also has three territories. She pauses at the computer and asks Stephanie whether this is the kind of information she needs for her Canada report.

pages.text: Subject: My questions Hi Jacqueline, Good to hear from you. Here, let me list some of the topics that my teacher wants covered in the report so that you have a better idea of what information I am looking for: people, economics, government, history, culture, religion, and physical geography. Hope that’s not too much. So, what’s your family like? My dad sells animal feed and my mom is a waitress at the truck stop outside of town. Do you have any brothers or sisters? I don’t. Thanks so much for doing this, and I can’t wait to tell you about Omaha and the United States for your report next month. Your friend, Stephanie.
pages.brief: Stephanie sits at a desk in Omaha and writes to Jacqueline. She asks about many report topics and describes her family: her father sells animal feed, and her mother is a waitress at a truck stop outside town. Stephanie has no brothers or sisters.

pages.text: Subject: My family Hey Stephanie, Wow, that is a lot of information to cover! How about this: I’ll start by talking about my family (that will at least cover your “people” section) and then maybe that will help answer some of the other sections. Okay? My dad is a fisherman in English Bay. He leaves before I wake up for school because he says he has to get to the Bay before the fish wake up! Vancouver has the largest port in North America, as far as exports go. It also rarely freezes, so my dad works year-round.
pages.brief: Jacqueline writes at her computer in Vancouver, smiling as she describes her father, a fisherman who leaves before dawn for English Bay. In the harbor, fishing boats sit on water that rarely freezes, and her father works year-round in North America’s largest port.

pages.text: Fish are a major resource here. My dad says Canada exports about 80 percent of its fish. Other resources are iron ore, nickel, zinc, copper, gold, silver, coal, and oil. I found that information online at Statistics Canada (you may want to check it out). My mom drives my brother and me to school every day. She’s a French teacher (both English and French are the official languages here) at my brother’s school. He’s in 12th grade, so next year he will go to college. Some of my classmates take the bus or the train to get to school, and a few ride their bikes. School starts at 8:30 and ends at 3:00.
pages.brief: Jacqueline’s mother drives Jacqueline and her twelfth-grade brother to school in Vancouver. Outside, classmates board a bus, train, or bicycle before school begins at 8:30. Fishing boats and piles of iron ore, nickel, copper, gold, coal, and oil show Canada’s resources.

pages.text: I’m in 4th grade, like you, and my most favorite class is social studies. Right now we’re studying the Canadian government, lucky for you! Let me give you some facts about the government from my notebook. Canada is a democracy, a government run by the people, just like the United States. We have our own constitution and our own bill of rights. The United States is a republic, but Canada is a constitutional monarchy in which the king or queen of England is our chief of state. The prime minister leads Parliament (no president here). Canada’s Parliament is made up of two houses, the Senate with 105 members and the House of Commons with 308 members. Hope that helps a little. I have to go (my mom is calling me because it’s time for lacrosse practice). I’ll try to answer the rest of your questions when I get back. Talk to you soon, Jacqueline.
pages.brief: Jacqueline, a fourth grader, sits with her social studies notebook and writes about Canada’s government. She shows a democracy with a constitution and Parliament’s two houses, then looks up as her mother calls from the doorway because it is time for lacrosse practice.

pages.text: Subject: Lacrosse? Hi Jacqueline, Thanks so much. What’s lacrosse? Is it like soccer? That’s what I play. My mom was wondering where your grandparents are from. My grandparents are from Germany. What do you do for fun? Every summer, my family goes to Florida and relaxes on the beach. Do you take any family vacations? Canada sounds so cool. Hope practice was fun. Your friend, Stephanie.
pages.brief: Stephanie writes from Omaha with a soccer ball beside her, asking Jacqueline about lacrosse. She mentions her German grandparents and her family’s summer trips to a Florida beach, where they relax together. Her friendly questions show curiosity about Canada and family vacations.

pages.text: Subject: Family heritage, family vacation Hi Stephanie, Practice was tough, I’m pretty tired, but I think I’m even more hungry. My mom is upstairs cooking dinner—we’re having caribou. She learned how to make it from my grandpa who was Inuit. Looks like I’m starting to answer your family heritage questions. Before I do that, I should tell you that, yes, I do play soccer but only in gym class, and it’s not as fun as lacrosse. Lacrosse is kind of like soccer, but we use sticks with baskets on the end to pass the ball to another player or hopefully into a goal that’s much smaller than a soccer goal.
pages.brief: Jacqueline comes home tired and hungry after lacrosse practice, carrying a stick with a basket on the end. Upstairs, her mother cooks caribou stew, a recipe learned from Jacqueline’s Inuit grandpa. Jacqueline explains how lacrosse players pass the ball and aim at a small goal.

pages.text: Okay, back to my family. My dad’s ancestors are from England. He can trace them as far back as the Klondike Gold Rush of 1897! My mother’s father was Inuit, like I said, but her mother was of French descent — and that’s why she knows French so well. To answer your religion question, most Canadians are Roman Catholic. Many others are Protestant, like us, or another Christian religion. Only a small number of people are Muslim, Jewish, Buddhist, or Hindu.
pages.brief: Jacqueline talks about her family heritage: her father’s English ancestors during the Klondike Gold Rush, her Inuit grandfather, and her French-descended grandmother. Nearby, church scenes show Roman Catholic and Protestant Canadians, with smaller groups of Muslim, Jewish, Buddhist, and Hindu people.

pages.text: Yes, we take family vacations. This past summer we went to Mount Logan in the Yukon’s Kluane National Park. The mountain rises to 5,959 meters (19,551 feet to you), which makes it the highest point in Canada. I was hoping that we would travel all the way around the country, all 9,984,670 square kilometers (or 3,854,045 square miles), but my mom and dad said that was too far. Did you know that Canada is the second largest country in the world?
pages.brief: Jacqueline and her family stand before Mount Logan in Yukon’s Kluane National Park, a towering snowy peak. She looks across the vast landscape, imagining travel all around Canada, the second-largest country in the world, though her parents say the whole country is too far.

pages.text: Canada has eight land regions: the Canadian Shield, the Hudson Bay Lowlands, the Western Cordillera, the Interior Lowlands, the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Lowlands, the Appalachians, the Arctic Lowlands, and the Innuitians. Since we headed straight north from Vancouver, we stayed in the Western Cordillera land region. The scenery in this region is amazing. There are so many mountains (I hope this is helping with your “physical geography” section).
pages.brief: Jacqueline and her family travel north from Vancouver through the Western Cordillera, surrounded by dramatic mountain scenery. Canada’s eight land regions are shown around them, including the Canadian Shield and Hudson Bay Lowlands, as Jacqueline looks out at the towering peaks of the Western Cordillera.

pages.text: The two regions I really want to see sometime in my life are the Canadian Shield and the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Lowlands. The Canadian Shield is the largest land region in Canada—it covers about half of the country! There are plains, mountains, and many ancient rocks there. The Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Lowlands is mostly rolling lowlands. This is where Niagara Falls and Canada’s main river, the St. Lawrence Seaway, are located. This area is often called Canada’s heartland because it is a center for agricultural production and industry (isn’t that kind of like Omaha?). Dinner’s ready, so I have to run (it smells great). As soon as I’m done, I’ll finish answering the rest of your questions. Here I come, caribou stew! Jacqueline.
pages.brief: Jacqueline writes about two regions she hopes to see: the rocky Canadian Shield and the rolling Great Lakes–St. Lawrence Lowlands, with Niagara Falls and the St. Lawrence Seaway. She imagines farms and industry before her mother calls her to dinner, caribou stew waiting.

pages.text: Subject: Caribou or Moose? Hi Jacqueline, I had no idea Canada was so big, and I’ve never heard of caribou. Online, they look like moose. Is that true? We have lots of deer here. Sometimes my friends and I see them in our backyards. What are your friends like? Talk with you soon. Your friend, Stephanie.
pages.brief: Stephanie sits at a computer in Omaha, surprised by how large Canada is and studying an online picture of a caribou that reminds her of a moose. Outside her window, deer stand in a backyard as she asks Jacqueline what her friends are like.

pages.text: Subject: Come visit! Hi Stephanie, Many of my friends are on the lacrosse team, but my best friend Li is not. He’s from China. Did you know that a lot of people immigrate to Canada from Asian countries? Each year when school starts, I look around my classroom and see more kids who are Asian. I worked on an immigration graph with Li in Math class last year that showed the number of people who came to Canada in 2003. I am sending you a copy of the graph we made (my mom helped me scan it to the computer). If you can’t open it, please let me know. Pakistan 12,330 India 24,560 People’s Republic of China 36,116 Sri Lanka 4,442 Philippines 11,978 S. Korea 7,086 United States 5,990 Iran 5,648 Romania 5,465 United Kingdom 5,194.
pages.brief: Jacqueline and her best friend Li, who is from China, work together in math class on a bar graph about immigration to Canada. Around them, classmates from Asian countries gather, and Jacqueline prepares a copy of their graph to send to Stephanie.

pages.text: You know what? I just looked at your original list of things your teacher wanted for this report, and I think we talked about all of them, except for history. I’ll go bug my dad for that (he’s a big history buff). Here, he just scanned me a timeline from one of his history books. I’ll attach it, too. 9,000 b.c. Artifacts show that native Canadians are living in the present-day Ontario area. a.d. 986 The first European, a Viking named Bjarni Herjolfsson, sees the Labrador coastline. 1608 Samuel de Champlain (“Father of New France”) founds Quebec City, which is the first permanent French settlement in Canada. 1610 Henry Hudson explores Hudson Bay. 1702 The French and British battle in Queen Anne’s War. 1818 The Canada–U.S. border is established at the 49th parallel. 1841 An Act of Union brings together Upper and Lower Canada, creating the Province of Canada. 1867 Sir John A. Macdonald is the first Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada. 1897 The gold rush begins in the Yukon. 1931 Great Britain gives Canada full authority over legislative matters. 1965 Canada issues a new flag. 1989 The Canada–U.S. Free Trade Agreement starts. 1999 The Inuit Territory of Nunavut is created.
pages.brief: Scenes from Canada’s past appear together: native Canadians in ancient Ontario, Viking Bjarni Herjolfsson sighting Labrador, Samuel de Champlain founding Quebec City, Henry Hudson exploring Hudson Bay, a French-British battle, the 49th-parallel border, Sir John A. Macdonald, the Yukon gold rush, a new flag, and Nunavut.

pages.text: Hope I helped you with your report. Maybe this next summer, you could persuade your family to come visit Canada instead of Florida. You could visit Ottawa (the national capital) or Toronto (the largest city), but let’s face it, Vancouver is the prettiest place to be in the summer. You’d love it. Can’t wait to hear about Omaha and the United States next month. Take care. Your friend, Jacqueline.
pages.brief: Jacqueline writes from Vancouver, encouraging Stephanie to persuade her family to visit Canada instead of Florida. She imagines Stephanie in Ottawa, the national capital, or Toronto, the largest city, while insisting Vancouver is the prettiest place in summer.

pages.text: 12 people from whom one descends caribou page 15 a type of large reindeer that lives in very cold places constitution page 9 basic laws of a state or nation that tell how the government is run constitutional monarchy page 9 a government in which a parliament monarchy oversees the power of a king or queen democracy page 9 a government in which the people vote for other people to represent them heritage page 11 something that is passed down from generation to generation Glossary Inuit page 11 a member of a group of native peoples living near the Arctic, such as northern Canada, Greenland, or Alaska Parliament page 9 a group of government officials who can make and change a nation’s laws provinces page 5 lands divided up by a country republic page 9 a nation led by a president and governed by elected representatives territories page 5 lands controlled or owned by another country.
pages.brief: A set of small scenes illustrates key ideas: an Inuit family, a caribou in a cold place, ancestors and heritage passed down, a parliament building, a constitution, voting citizens in a democracy, and Canada’s provinces and territories.
